title: One Treat Now or Two Later?
paragraphs: Imagine you are four years old. A researcher places a marshmallow on the table in front of you and makes you an offer: you can eat it right now, or you can wait until she returns and get two. Then she walks out of the room, leaving you alone with the sweet. What would you do?

In the late 1960s, the scientist Walter Mischel [[initiated|L5-0464]] a set of tests like this at a school for young children at Stanford University. Not every child liked marshmallows, so, depending on each child's [[preference|L5-0647]], a cookie or another treat was used as a [[substitute|L5-0864]]. The researchers [[documented|L5-0307]] how long each of the [[participants|L5-0602]] could wait. Some ate the treat at once. Others covered their eyes, sang to themselves, or turned their backs on it. Simply looking at the treat, or catching its sweet [[scent|L5-0757]], could [[trigger|L5-0927]] a strong desire to eat it.

Years later, Mischel checked on some of the children. He found that, on average, those who had waited longer did better in school as teenagers. Many people [[derived|L5-0276]] a simple lesson from this: self-control is a [[trait|L5-0916]] you are born with, and it decides your future.

However, the story has [[evolved|L5-0351]]. In 2018, researchers tested a larger [[version|L5-0963]] of the study with children from a wider range of families. They found a much weaker link, and their results [[highlighted|L5-0431]] the role of a child's home life. Another study showed that when an adult broke a small promise just before the test, children waited for a shorter time. The most useful [[insight|L5-0473]] may be this: waiting is not only about self-control. It also depends on trust, and on simple tricks, like looking away, that anyone can learn.
zh: 想像你現在四歲。一位研究人員在你面前的桌上放了一顆棉花糖，並提出一個條件：你可以現在就吃掉它，也可以等她回來，那時就能得到兩顆。接著她走出房間，留下你獨自面對這顆糖。你會怎麼做？
1960 年代末期，科學家沃爾特・米歇爾在史丹佛大學的一所幼兒學校發起了一系列這樣的測試。並不是每個孩子都喜歡棉花糖，所以會依照每個孩子的偏好，改用餅乾或其他點心來代替。研究人員記錄下每位參與者能等多久。有些孩子馬上就把點心吃掉；有些則遮住眼睛、自己唱歌，或乾脆轉身背對點心。光是看著點心，或聞到它甜甜的香味，就足以引發強烈的想吃欲望。
多年後，米歇爾追蹤了其中一些孩子。他發現，平均而言，當年等得比較久的孩子，到了青少年時期在學校的表現比較好。許多人從中得出一個簡單的結論：自制力是一種與生俱來的特質，而且會決定你的未來。
然而，這個故事後來有了轉變。2018 年，研究人員以來自更多元家庭背景的孩子，進行了規模更大的版本。他們發現兩者的關聯弱了許多，而他們的結果也凸顯出孩子家庭生活所扮演的角色。另一項研究則顯示，如果大人在測試前剛剛對孩子失信，孩子等待的時間就會變短。最有用的啟示或許是：等待不只關乎自制力，也取決於信任，以及一些任何人都學得會的簡單技巧，例如把視線移開。

glosses.zh: 沃爾特・米歇爾（美國心理學家）

questions.stem: In Mischel's tests, what did the children have to decide?
options: Which of two adults they trusted more
Whether to share their treat with a friend
Whether to eat one treat now or wait to get two
questions.explain: 第一段說孩子可以馬上吃掉一顆，或等研究人員回來得到兩顆，故選 (C)。(D) 文中提到氣味會引發想吃的欲望，但孩子不需要比較哪個點心比較香。
questions.evidence: you can eat it right now, or you can wait until she returns and get two

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what did some children do while they waited?
options: They covered their eyes or turned away from the treat.
They asked the researcher to come back early.
They hid the treat under the table.
They traded their treat for a cookie.
questions.explain: 第二段說有些孩子遮住眼睛、自己唱歌，或轉身背對點心，故選 (A)。(D) 餅乾是依孩子的偏好用來代替棉花糖，不是孩子拿點心去換的。
questions.evidence: Others covered their eyes, sang to themselves, or turned their backs on it.

questions.stem: The word "derived" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
options: got or took from a source
questions.explain: 許多人「從這項發現」得出自制力是天生特質的結論，derive A from B 指「從 B 得到 A」，故選 (D)。(A)、(C) 都是不接受的意思，和後面接著說出的結論不合。
questions.evidence: Many people derived a simple lesson from this

questions.stem: Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
options: Children who eat the treat at once will fail in school.
A child's ability to wait is shaped by his or her situation and can be improved.
The first marshmallow tests were completely wrong.
Self-control is a trait that cannot be changed.
questions.explain: 最後一段說等待也取決於信任和家庭生活，而且移開視線等技巧任何人都學得會，可知作者認為等待能力受環境影響、也能改善，故選 (B)。(D) 正是第三段說的舊看法，作者在最後一段已加以修正。
questions.evidence: It also depends on trust, and on simple tricks, like looking away, that anyone can learn.

vocab.stem: The new hotel can ______ up to 800 guests, so it is often used for large events.
vocab.explain: 飯店能「容納」多達 800 位客人，故選 accommodate。facilitate（促進）、derive（取得；源自）、initiate（發起）都不能用來表示空間容納多少人。

vocab.stem: Our school holds a graduation ______ every June to celebrate the students' hard work.
vocab.explain: 每年六月舉行畢業「典禮」，graduation ceremony 是固定說法，故選 ceremony。sensation（感覺；轟動）、consumption（消耗）、innovation（創新）都不是學校會「舉行」的活動。

title: Living Lights of the Deep Sea
paragraphs: Far below the surface of the ocean, where light from the sun never reaches, the water is completely dark—or so it seems. In fact, the deep sea is full of tiny flashes of blue light. Many of the animals living there can produce their own light, an [[extraordinary|L5-0374]] ability called bioluminescence.

These animals [[generate|L5-0405]] light through a chemical reaction inside their bodies, and they use it in clever ways. Some fish have a long, thin part on the head, like a fishing [[rod|L5-0746]], with a glowing tip that draws smaller fish close enough to be eaten. Certain shrimp shoot out a cloud of glowing liquid to confuse their enemies and escape. For animals [[confined|L5-0199]] to such a dark world, light is [[crucial|L5-0245]] for finding food and staying alive. Scientists believe this [[trait|L5-0916]] has [[evolved|L5-0351]] separately many times in different groups of sea animals.

Studying these [[residents|L5-0726]] of the deep is not easy. [[Exploration|L5-0368]] of the deep sea requires special machines, and a single [[expedition|L5-0364]] can last for weeks. Bright white lights tend to scare animals away, so the [[marine|L5-0523]] scientist Edith Widder, who has [[dedicated|L5-0262]] her career to studying light in the ocean, designed a camera system that uses red light, which many deep-sea animals cannot see. She also built an [[innovative|L5-0470]] tool: a fake jellyfish that flashes blue lights. In 2012, it helped a team film a giant squid in its natural home for the first time. When the video was shown on TV, [[viewers|L5-0970]] around the world were amazed.

Each new discovery gives scientists fresh [[insight|L5-0473]] into how life survives in one of the most difficult places on Earth. Yet large parts of the deep sea have still not been explored. Who knows what other glowing animals are waiting in the dark?
zh: 在海面下很深的地方，陽光永遠照不到，海水一片漆黑——至少看起來是如此。事實上，深海裡充滿了微小的藍色閃光。許多住在那裡的動物都能自己發光，這種非凡的能力叫做生物發光。
這些動物透過體內的化學反應產生光，並用很聰明的方式加以運用。有些魚的頭上有一根細長的構造，像一根釣竿，末端會發光，能把小魚引誘到夠近的地方再吃掉。某些蝦子會噴出一團發光的液體，讓敵人搞不清楚狀況，趁機逃走。對被困在如此黑暗世界中的動物來說，光對覓食和存活都極為重要。科學家認為，這項特徵在不同的海洋動物類群中，已經各自獨立演化出現過許多次。
研究這些深海居民並不容易。探索深海需要特殊的機器，一趟探險航程可能長達好幾週。明亮的白光往往會把動物嚇跑，因此畢生致力於研究海洋光線的海洋科學家伊迪絲・威德，設計了一套使用紅光的攝影系統，而許多深海動物看不見紅光。她還做了一個創新的工具：一隻會閃藍光的假水母。2012 年，這個工具幫助一支團隊首度在大王魷魚的自然棲息處拍下牠的身影。影片在電視上播出時，全世界的觀眾都驚嘆不已。
每一項新發現，都讓科學家對生命如何在地球上最艱困的地方之一存活下來，有了新的洞見。然而，深海仍有大片區域尚未被探索。誰知道還有哪些會發光的動物，正在黑暗中等待著呢？

glosses.zh: 魷魚（giant squid 大王魷魚）

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do certain shrimp protect themselves?
options: By shooting out a cloud of glowing liquid
By using a glowing part on the head
questions.explain: 第二段說某些蝦子會噴出一團發光的液體來迷惑敵人並逃走，故選 (B)。(D) 頭上像釣竿的發光構造是某些魚用來引誘獵物的。

questions.stem: Why does Edith Widder's camera system use red light?
options: Red light travels farther in water than blue light.
Red light makes the animals glow more brightly.
Many deep-sea animals cannot see red light, so it does not scare them away.
Red light was the only color her camera could use.
questions.explain: 第三段說明亮的白光會把動物嚇跑，所以她改用許多深海動物看不見的紅光，故選 (C)。(A)、(B)、(D) 文中都沒有提到。

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does "it" in "it helped a team film a giant squid" refer to?
questions.explain: it 指前一句提到的創新工具，也就是會閃藍光的假水母，故選 (A)。(D) 影片是拍攝之後才有的，不可能幫忙拍攝。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why the deep sea is too dangerous to explore
How fish catch food near the surface of the ocean
The life story of a famous TV reporter
How deep-sea animals make and use light, and how scientists study them
questions.explain: 全文介紹深海動物如何發光、怎麼利用光，以及科學家如何研究牠們，故選 (D)。(A) 文中只說探索不容易，並沒有說太危險而不能探索。

vocab.stem: Getting enough sleep is ______ for students who want to stay healthy and do well in school.
vocab.explain: 充足的睡眠對想保持健康、學業表現好的學生「至關重要」，故選 crucial。indigenous（原住民的；本土的）、excessive（過度的）、marine（海洋的）放進句中語意都不通。

title: Before You Hit Share
paragraphs: A photo appears on your phone: a shark swimming down a flooded highway after a big storm. Your friends are sharing it, and the comments are full of [[astonishment|L5-0064]]. It looks real. However, the same picture has appeared online after many different storms for years, and experts have shown that it was made by combining two separate photos.

Why do people believe stories like this? Part of the reason is the way the brain works. To save energy, our [[cognitive|L5-0150]] system often chooses the easiest path. We tend to accept information that matches what we already believe, and we react quickly to anything that [[triggers|L5-0927]] fear or surprise. False stories are often [[elaborate|L5-0323]], full of exciting details, and [[hence|L5-0428]] easy to remember and fun to share. In fact, one large study of social media found that false news traveled farther and faster than true news.

Fortunately, many people are taking the [[initiative|L5-0465]] to fight back. In Taiwan and around the world, fact-checking groups examine popular claims and explain which ones are true. They interview [[specialists|L5-0815]], such as doctors and scientists, to find out what the scientific [[consensus|L5-0204]] is, and they [[highlight|L5-0431]] the tricks most often used to fool readers.

You can check, too. Use [[caution|L5-0122]] when a post promises a medical [[breakthrough|L5-0103]] that seems too good to be true. Look for the original source, and see whether trusted news reports tell the same story. Search for older [[versions|L5-0963]] of a picture; an image [[depicting|L5-0272]] "today's flood" may have been taken years ago in another country. Above all, if a post makes you feel strong anger or fear, pause. A few seconds of checking is [[crucial|L5-0245]] before you hit "share."
zh: 你的手機跳出一張照片：一場大暴風雨過後，一條鯊魚在淹水的高速公路上游動。朋友們紛紛轉傳，留言裡滿是驚訝。它看起來很真實。然而，同一張照片多年來在許多不同的暴風雨過後都曾在網路上出現，而專家已經證明，它是把兩張不同的照片合成的。
人們為什麼會相信這類故事？部分原因在於大腦運作的方式。為了節省能量，我們的認知系統常常選擇最省力的路。我們傾向接受符合自己既有想法的資訊，也會對任何引發恐懼或驚訝的事物迅速做出反應。假消息往往經過精心編造、充滿刺激的細節，因此容易記住、轉傳起來也很有趣。事實上，一項針對社群媒體的大型研究發現，假新聞比真新聞傳得更遠、更快。
幸好，許多人正主動採取行動來反擊。在台灣和世界各地，事實查核團體會檢驗流傳甚廣的說法，並說明哪些是真的。他們訪問醫生、科學家等專家，弄清楚科學界的共識是什麼，並特別點出最常被用來欺騙讀者的手法。
你也可以自己查證。如果一則貼文宣稱有好得令人難以置信的醫學突破，要小心。去找原始來源，看看可信的新聞報導是否說法一致。搜尋一張照片的較早版本；一張描繪「今天水災」的照片，可能是多年前在別的國家拍的。最重要的是，如果一則貼文讓你感到強烈的憤怒或恐懼，先停一下。在你按下「分享」之前，花幾秒鐘查證是非常關鍵的。

questions.stem: What is true about the shark photo described in paragraph 1?
options: It was taken during the biggest storm in history.
It was first shared by a group of scientists.
It was made by putting two separate photos together.
It shows a real shark that swam onto a highway.
questions.explain: 第一段說專家已證明這張照片是把兩張不同的照片合成的，故選 (C)。(D) 正是許多人誤信的內容，與事實相反。
questions.evidence: it was made by combining two separate photos

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, which kind of information do people tend to accept?
options: Information that matches what they already believe
Information that comes from older friends
Information that makes them feel calm
questions.explain: 第二段說我們傾向接受符合自己既有想法的資訊，故選 (A)。(B) 與文意相反，文中說假消息常充滿刺激的細節，所以容易被記住。
questions.evidence: We tend to accept information that matches what we already believe

questions.stem: The word "consensus" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 事實查核團體訪問專家，是為了知道科學界普遍「同意」的看法是什麼，consensus 指「共識」，故選 (D)。(B) 強烈的懷疑與「共識」意思相反。
questions.evidence: to find out what the scientific consensus is

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To prove that all news on social media is false
To explain why false information spreads and how readers can check it
To introduce the history of fact-checking groups in Taiwan
To teach readers how to take better photos
questions.explain: 文章先舉假照片為例，再說明人們為何會相信假消息，最後介紹查核團體與讀者自己查證的方法，故選 (B)。(A) 說法太絕對，文中只說假新聞傳得較快，並未說所有新聞都是假的。
questions.evidence: You can check, too.

vocab.stem: Many animals are losing their natural ______ as forests are cut down to make room for roads and houses.
vocab.explain: 森林被砍伐，動物失去天然的「棲息地」，故選 habitats。rituals（儀式）、specialists（專家）、executives（主管）都不是動物會失去的生存環境。

vocab.stem: After studying for six hours, Amy felt a deep sense of ______ and decided to take a short walk.
vocab.explain: 連續讀書六小時後感到「疲勞」，所以去散步，故選 fatigue。behalf 只用於 on behalf of（代表），consensus（共識）、stock（存貨；股票）都不是個人的感受。

title: A Lucky Mess in the Lab
paragraphs: In September 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming returned to his lab in London after a summer holiday. Fleming [[specialized|L5-0816]] in the study of bacteria, and he was known for keeping a rather messy workplace. Before leaving, he had piled up a number of dishes in which he was growing bacteria. Now, as he sorted through them, something caught his eye.

On one dish, a spot of mold had grown. All around it was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. Many people would have thrown the dish away, but Fleming [[perceived|L5-0617]] that something important was happening: the mold seemed to produce a substance that killed bacteria. After careful [[inquiry|L5-0471]], he named it penicillin and [[documented|L5-0307]] his findings in a report in 1929. He had [[stumbled|L5-0858]] upon one of the greatest [[breakthroughs|L5-0103]] in medicine.

Yet for more than ten years, penicillin was not used to treat patients. Fleming could not produce it in large amounts or make it pure enough. Around 1940, a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain solved these problems. Soon factories in the United States began [[massive|L5-0526]] production, which [[rendered|L5-0719]] the medicine widely available. It saved a huge number of lives, and in 1945 the three men shared the Nobel Prize. Fleming never asked for a [[patent|L5-0608]] on his discovery.

In his Nobel speech, Fleming also gave a warning. If people took too little of the medicine, or took it when they did not need it, bacteria might change and learn to survive it. Seen from today's [[perspective|L5-0622]], his words were wise. Such bacteria have become a serious problem, and health experts [[reinforce|L5-0716]] his message: take this kind of medicine only when a doctor [[recommends|L5-0709]] it. Simple [[precautions|L5-0645]], such as washing your hands, are also [[crucial|L5-0245]].
zh: 1928 年 9 月，一位名叫亞歷山大・弗萊明的蘇格蘭醫生度完暑假，回到他在倫敦的實驗室。弗萊明專門研究細菌，而且出了名的不太愛整理工作環境。離開前，他把好幾個培養細菌的盤子堆在一起。現在，當他一一整理這些盤子時，有樣東西引起了他的注意。
其中一個盤子上長了一小塊黴菌。黴菌周圍有一圈透明的區域，那裡的細菌都死了。很多人可能會直接把盤子丟掉，但弗萊明察覺到有重要的事情正在發生：這種黴菌似乎會製造某種能殺死細菌的物質。經過仔細的探究，他將它命名為盤尼西林，並在 1929 年把研究結果記錄在一篇報告中。他無意間發現了醫學史上最重大的突破之一。
然而，在之後的十多年裡，盤尼西林並沒有被用來治療病人。弗萊明無法大量製造它，也無法讓它夠純。大約在 1940 年，牛津大學一支由霍華德・弗洛里和恩斯特・柴恩帶領的團隊解決了這些問題。不久之後，美國的工廠開始大規模生產，使這種藥得以廣泛使用。它拯救了非常多人的性命，1945 年這三人共同獲得諾貝爾獎。弗萊明從未替他的發現申請專利。
弗萊明在諾貝爾獎演說中也提出了警告：如果人們服用的藥量太少，或在不需要時服用，細菌可能會產生變化，學會在這種藥物下存活。從今天的角度來看，他的話很有遠見。這類細菌已成為嚴重的問題，而醫療專家也一再強調他的提醒：只有在醫生建議時才服用這類藥物。勤洗手等簡單的預防措施也非常重要。

questions.stem: What did Fleming notice on one of his dishes?
options: All the bacteria on it had grown much larger.
Someone had cleaned it while he was away.
It was the only dish without any bacteria.

title: Olives: A Small Fruit with a Long Story
paragraphs: Few foods have shaped human history like the [[olive|L5-0581]]. Today, olives and olive oil are at the heart of Mediterranean [[cuisine|L5-0249]], giving many dishes from Greece, Italy, and Spain their [[distinctive|L5-0304]] flavor. Yet people have been enjoying this small, bitter fruit for thousands of years.

Scientists believe olive trees were first grown for food more than 6,000 years ago near the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea. [[Fragments|L5-0396]] of clay jars that once held olive oil have been found at many ancient sites. Traders [[ventured|L5-0959]] across the sea in ships full of oil, and the trees soon spread to Greece, Italy, and North Africa. Even the English word "oil" is [[derived|L5-0276]] from an ancient Greek word for olive oil.

Olive oil was used for far more than cooking. People burned it in lamps for light, rubbed it on their skin, and poured it out in religious [[rituals|L5-0744]]. Because this golden [[fluid|L5-0389]] was so valuable, it was [[crucial|L5-0245]] to trade and daily life. Ancient writers even left [[descriptive|L5-0278]] notes on how to grow the trees and press the fruit. In Egypt, olive branches were found in the [[burial|L5-0112]] place of the young king Tutankhamun.

The Greeks [[perceived|L5-0617]] the olive tree as a gift from the gods. According to an old story, Athena, a [[warrior|L5-0982]] goddess, gave the first olive tree to the people of Athens, and the city was named after her. At the ancient Olympic Games, the [[ultimate|L5-0935]] prize was not gold but a simple crown of olive leaves. So the next time you taste an olive, remember that you are enjoying a little piece of history.
zh: 很少有食物像橄欖一樣影響了人類的歷史。今天，橄欖和橄欖油是地中海料理的核心，讓希臘、義大利和西班牙的許多菜餚擁有獨特的風味。然而，人們享用這種小小的、帶苦味的果實，已經有好幾千年了。
科學家認為，橄欖樹早在六千多年前，就在地中海東端附近開始被種來當作食物。在許多古代遺址，都發現了曾經裝過橄欖油的陶罐碎片。商人冒險搭乘載滿橄欖油的船隻橫渡大海，橄欖樹很快就傳到了希臘、義大利和北非。就連英文的 oil（油）這個字，也是源自古希臘文中指橄欖油的字。
橄欖油的用途遠遠不只烹飪。人們把它放在油燈裡燃燒照明、抹在皮膚上，也在宗教儀式中倒出來使用。由於這種金黃色的液體非常珍貴，它對貿易和日常生活都至關重要。古代的作家甚至留下了詳細描述的筆記，說明如何種植橄欖樹和壓榨果實。在埃及，年輕法老圖坦卡門的墓中也發現了橄欖枝。
希臘人把橄欖樹視為眾神的禮物。根據一則古老的故事，戰爭女神雅典娜把第一棵橄欖樹送給雅典人，這座城市也因此以她命名。在古代奧運會上，最高的獎品不是黃金，而是一頂用橄欖葉編成的簡單頭冠。所以下次你吃到橄欖時，記得你正在品嚐的，是一小段歷史。

title: When Farms Move into the City
paragraphs: More than half of the world's people now live in cities, and the number keeps growing. Most of the food they eat, however, is grown far away and must travel long distances by truck, ship, or plane before it reaches their plates. Some cities are now trying a different approach: bringing the farm to the people.

City farming comes in many forms. In some neighborhoods, [[residents|L5-0726]] turn empty land into shared gardens. In others, vegetables are grown on the tops of buildings. One of the most [[innovative|L5-0470]] ideas is the "vertical farm," in which plants grow indoors in [[layers|L5-0502]], one above another, under special lights. Instead of soil, many of these farms use water mixed with plant food as a [[substitute|L5-0864]].

Supporters say these farms offer several advantages. Because the food is grown close to where it is eaten, it stays fresh, and less fuel is needed to carry it, which cuts the [[consumption|L5-0211]] of oil. Indoor farms are [[shielded|L5-0782]] from storms and insects, so crops can be grown all year round with little or no chemical spray. Many indoor farms also save water by collecting it and using it again. For children, a school garden can [[boost|L5-0097]] interest in healthy eating.

However, city farming is not a perfect answer. The lights [[generate|L5-0405]] large electricity bills, and land in cities is expensive. Several companies that [[ventured|L5-0959]] into indoor farming have run out of money. Most indoor farms grow only greens such as lettuce, because crops like rice and wheat need too much space and light. In addition, soil in old city areas can contain harmful metals, a [[hazard|L5-0426]] that gardeners must test for.

From a wider [[perspective|L5-0622]], city farms will not replace the countryside. Still, they play a [[crucial|L5-0245]] role in helping city people learn where their food comes from. Successful projects often depend on [[collaboration|L5-0153]] among city governments, schools, and local groups. The [[ultimate|L5-0935]] goal is not to grow every vegetable in the city, but to build a food system that is fresher, closer, and stronger.
zh: 全世界有一半以上的人口現在住在城市裡，而且人數還在持續增加。然而，他們吃的食物大多種在遙遠的地方，必須靠卡車、船隻或飛機長途運送，才能送上他們的餐桌。現在有些城市正在嘗試另一種做法：把農場帶到人們身邊。
城市農業有許多形式。在某些社區，居民把空地變成共享的菜園；在另一些地方，蔬菜種在大樓的屋頂上。其中最創新的構想之一是「垂直農場」：植物在室內一層層地往上排列生長，並使用特殊的燈光照明。許多這類農場不用土壤，而是用混合了植物養分的水來代替。
支持者說，這些農場有好幾項優點。因為食物就種在吃的地方附近，所以能保持新鮮，運送所需的燃料也比較少，可以減少石油的消耗。室內農場不受暴風雨和昆蟲侵擾，所以一年四季都能種植作物，而且幾乎不必噴灑化學藥劑。許多室內農場也會把水收集起來重複使用，藉此節省用水。對孩子來說，學校菜園也能提高他們對健康飲食的興趣。
然而，城市農業並不是完美的解答。照明會產生高額的電費，城市的土地也很昂貴。有好幾家投入室內農業的公司已經把錢用光了。大多數室內農場只種萵苣之類的葉菜，因為稻米、小麥等作物需要太多空間和光線。此外，舊市區的土壤可能含有有害的金屬，這是種菜的人必須事先檢測的危險。
從更宏觀的角度來看，城市農場不會取代鄉間的農田。儘管如此，它們在幫助城市居民了解食物從何而來這件事上，扮演了關鍵的角色。成功的計畫往往有賴市政府、學校和地方團體之間的合作。最終的目標並不是在城市裡種出每一種蔬菜，而是建立一個更新鮮、更貼近人們，也更穩固的糧食系統。

title: Broken Bowls, Bright Roofs
paragraphs: Look up at the roof of an old temple in Taiwan, and you may see an amazing scene: bright dragons, flowers, and figures from famous stories, all shining in the sun. Many of these decorations are made with a traditional method called jiannian, which means "cut and paste." Workers cut colorful bowls into small pieces, then press the [[fragments|L5-0396]] one by one into a [[layer|L5-0502]] of wet plaster shaped like the figure they want.

The craft came to Taiwan with settlers from southern China long ago and slowly developed its own [[distinctive|L5-0304]] style here. On a [[sacred|L5-0747]] building like a temple, each figure is [[symbolic|L5-0882]]. A dragon may stand for power and good luck, while certain fruits express the hope for an [[abundant|L5-0006]] harvest, a wish that mattered greatly in an [[agricultural|L5-0030]] society. Sadly, many of the people who created these works remain [[anonymous|L5-0045]], since their names were rarely recorded.

Today, this art faces serious problems. Sun, wind, and rain slowly damage the pieces. When old temples are repaired, some original works are replaced with new ones, which can [[alter|L5-0040]] the look of the whole building. There is also a [[shortage|L5-0784]] of young people willing to [[inherit|L5-0463]] the skill, because it takes years of practice and the pay is low. Experts [[anticipate|L5-0046]] that, without help, the loss of this knowledge will [[accelerate|L5-0008]].

Fortunately, the government has [[acknowledged|L5-0014]] jiannian as an important traditional craft, and some masters now teach classes. Some temples also keep [[antique|L5-0047]] pieces on display so that visitors can see them up close. You do not need special training to start. With [[ample|L5-0043]] patience, anyone can learn to turn broken bowls into something beautiful.
zh: 抬頭看看台灣老廟的屋頂，你可能會看到令人驚豔的景象：色彩鮮豔的龍、花朵和故事裡的人物，全都在陽光下閃閃發亮。這些裝飾有許多是用一種叫做「剪黏」的傳統技法做成的，意思就是「剪下再黏上」。師傅把彩色的碗剪成小片，再把這些碎片一片一片地壓進塑成人物形狀的濕灰泥層中。
這項技藝很久以前隨著中國南方的移民來到台灣，並在這裡逐漸發展出自己獨特的風格。在廟宇這樣神聖的建築上，每個圖案都具有象徵意義。龍可能代表力量與好運，某些水果則表達對豐收的期盼——在農業社會裡，這樣的願望非常重要。可惜的是，創作這些作品的許多人至今仍不知姓名，因為他們的名字很少被記錄下來。
如今，這項藝術面臨嚴重的問題。陽光、風雨會慢慢損壞這些碎片。老廟整修時，有些原本的作品會被新作品取代，可能改變整座建築的樣貌。此外，願意傳承這門技藝的年輕人也很缺乏，因為它需要多年的練習，收入又低。專家預料，如果沒有外界的幫助，這些知識流失的速度將會加快。
幸好，政府已經認可剪黏是重要的傳統工藝，有些師傅現在也開設課程教學。有些廟宇也會展出古老的剪黏作品，讓參觀者近距離欣賞。你不需要受過特別的訓練就能開始學。只要有充分的耐心，任何人都能學會把破碗變成美麗的作品。

title: Join Our Team of Young Street Guides
paragraphs: Do you love history, enjoy meeting people, and want to show visitors the hidden side of our city? The Harbor City Culture [[Bureau|L5-0110]] is looking for high school students to join our Young Guides program this summer.

About the area: Our Old Town grew quickly during a trade [[boom|L5-0096]] about a hundred years ago. Within its [[boundaries|L5-0101]], you will find an [[array|L5-0055]] of [[colonial|L5-0156]]-era buildings, small family shops, and a temple more than 150 years old. Several of the buildings were designed by a well-known [[architect|L5-0051]] who mixed Western and Taiwanese styles. Tour [[highlights|L5-0431]] include a tea house with its original wooden windows and a street of red-brick shops.

What you will do: lead 40-minute walking tours on Saturday or Sunday mornings, answer visitors' questions, and hang [[banners|L5-0077]] and set up the welcome table before each tour. Who can apply: students aged 15 to 18 who can speak clearly in Chinese and English and are free for at least six weekends in July and August. Do not make the [[assumption|L5-0063]] that you must already be a history expert. All [[participants|L5-0602]] will attend two training days led by local history [[specialists|L5-0815]].

Why join? Being a guide is [[beneficial|L5-0083]] in many ways. You will build your [[capability|L5-0117]] to speak in front of groups, make friends who share your interests, and receive a thank-you letter from the Bureau at the end of the summer. Our guides work as a [[collective|L5-0154]], so you will never be alone. Please note that summer days can be very hot, so be [[cautious|L5-0123]]: bring water and a hat to every tour. To apply, fill out the form on our website by June 10. We look forward to meeting you!
zh: 你熱愛歷史、喜歡認識新朋友，又想讓遊客看見我們城市不為人知的一面嗎？港城文化局正在招募高中生，加入今年暑假的「青年導覽員」計畫。
關於導覽區域：我們的老城區大約在一百年前的一波貿易熱潮中迅速發展。在它的範圍內，你會看到一系列殖民時期的建築、小小的家族商店，以及一座超過 150 年歷史的廟宇。其中有幾棟建築出自一位知名建築師之手，他融合了西式與台灣的風格。導覽的精彩重點包括一間保留原始木窗的茶館，以及一整條紅磚店屋街。
工作內容：在週六或週日上午帶領 40 分鐘的徒步導覽、回答遊客的問題，並在每場導覽前掛好布條、布置迎賓桌。申請資格：15 至 18 歲、能以中文和英文清楚表達，且七、八月間至少有六個週末可以參加的學生。不要以為你必須已經是歷史專家。所有參加者都會參加兩天的培訓，由在地歷史專家帶領。
為什麼要加入？擔任導覽員有許多好處。你能培養在眾人面前說話的能力、結交志同道合的朋友，並在暑假結束時收到文化局的感謝函。我們的導覽員以團隊方式合作，所以你絕不會孤單一人。請注意，夏天可能非常炎熱，請小心：每次導覽都要帶水和帽子。報名請於 6 月 10 日前填寫我們網站上的表單。期待與你見面！

title: The Poems on the 7:10 Bus
paragraphs: Every morning, Ting [[commuted|L5-0167]] to school on the 7:10 bus. The other [[commuters|L5-0168]] stared at their phones, and Ting usually did the same. At school, she tried hard to [[conform|L5-0200]]. She laughed at the same jokes as everyone else and rarely said what she really thought. But in the back of her notebook, she kept a secret: dozens of short poems about the city waking up outside the window.

One rainy Monday, an old man sitting across from her was reading a book of [[contemporary|L5-0215]] poetry. Noticing Ting looking at the cover, he asked, "Do you write?" Ting almost said no. Instead, she heard herself say, "A little," and felt herself [[blush|L5-0092]]. The man turned out to be a retired teacher who held a poetry reading at the library every month. With a [[compassionate|L5-0172]] smile, he invited her to read at the next one. Ting politely [[declined|L5-0261]]. The idea of standing in front of strangers made her stomach turn.

For weeks, she could not stop thinking about it. Something [[compelled|L5-0174]] her to open the notebook again and again. Finally, she decided to [[confront|L5-0201]] her fear and made a [[commitment|L5-0163]] to herself: one poem, one minute, no running away. On the bus each day, she practiced quietly.

On the night of her [[debut|L5-0256]], a moment she had long [[anticipated|L5-0046]], her hands shook as she stepped up to the microphone. She read a poem about the 7:10 bus: the sleepy faces, the rain on the glass, the kind words of a stranger. When she finished, the room was silent. Then the old man began to clap, and the clapping proved [[contagious|L5-0212]]. Ting felt a warm [[sensation|L5-0767]] spread through her chest. The next morning, she did not look at her phone. She took out her notebook and began to write.
zh: 每天早上，婷都搭 7 點 10 分的公車通勤上學。其他通勤族都盯著手機看，婷通常也一樣。在學校，她很努力地讓自己跟大家一樣：和所有人一起笑同樣的笑話，也很少說出自己真正的想法。但在筆記本的最後幾頁，她藏著一個祕密：好幾十首短詩，寫的是窗外正在甦醒的城市。
一個下雨的星期一，坐在她對面的老先生正在讀一本當代詩集。他注意到婷在看書的封面，便問：「妳寫詩嗎？」婷差點就說沒有，卻聽見自己說：「寫一點點。」同時感覺到自己臉紅了。原來這位老先生是一位退休老師，每個月都在圖書館舉辦朗詩會。他帶著溫和體貼的微笑，邀請她在下一次的朗詩會上朗讀。婷禮貌地婉拒了。光是想到要站在一群陌生人面前，就讓她胃裡一陣翻騰。
然而，好幾個星期，她都忍不住一直想著這件事。某種力量驅使她一次又一次地翻開筆記本。最後，她決定面對自己的恐懼，並對自己許下承諾：一首詩、一分鐘、絕不逃跑。每天在公車上，她都小聲地練習。
到了她初次登台的那個晚上，也就是她期待已久的時刻，她走上前站到麥克風前，雙手不停發抖。她朗讀了一首關於 7 點 10 分公車的詩：一張張睏倦的臉、玻璃上的雨水，以及一位陌生人親切的話語。她唸完時，全場一片寂靜。接著，老先生開始拍手，掌聲很快就傳遍了整個房間。婷感覺一股暖意流遍胸口。第二天早上，她沒有看手機。她拿出筆記本，開始寫作。

title: The Real Price of a Cheap Shirt
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, most clothing stores offered new styles a few times a year. Today, some fashion [[enterprises|L5-0329]] put new designs on their shelves almost every week. This model, known as fast fashion, has changed how young people shop. A shirt that costs less than a lunch is easy to pick up on the way home from an [[errand|L5-0342]], and many shoppers [[embrace|L5-0326]] the chance to try a new look without spending much money.

However, cheap clothes come with hidden costs. Producing [[fabric|L5-0375]] uses huge amounts of water, and some of the dyes that give clothes their bright colors are [[toxic|L5-0915]]. When factories pour dirty water into rivers, these chemicals [[dissolve|L5-0302]] and spread, harming fish and the whole river [[ecosystem|L5-0321]]. Low prices also depend on low pay. Some factory workers work long hours for very little money, which raises serious [[ethical|L5-0349]] questions. Many companies do not [[disclose|L5-0296]] where or how their clothes are made, so shoppers have no easy way to find out.

The problems continue after we buy. Because the clothes are so cheap, people often buy far more than they need, and this [[excessive|L5-0355]] [[consumption|L5-0211]] creates mountains of waste. We feel good when we [[donate|L5-0311]] old clothes to charity, but charities receive far more [[donations|L5-0312]] than they can sell, and much of the rest is shipped to other countries, burned, or thrown away.

Still, there are signs of change. Many young shoppers are [[enthusiastic|L5-0330]] about buying used clothes, repairing what they already own, or trading clothes with friends. They make a clear [[distinction|L5-0303]] between what they want and what they really need. Looking good does not have to be [[exclusive|L5-0358]] to people who buy something new every week. So before you buy your next shirt, ask yourself: Will I wear this at least thirty times?
zh: 二十年前，大多數服飾店一年只推出幾次新款。如今，有些時尚企業幾乎每週都把新設計擺上貨架。這種模式被稱為「快時尚」，它改變了年輕人購物的方式。一件比一頓午餐還便宜的襯衫，在辦完事回家的路上就能順手買下，許多消費者也樂於把握機會，不必花大錢就能嘗試新造型。
然而，便宜的衣服背後藏著代價。生產布料要用掉大量的水，而一些讓衣服色彩鮮豔的染料是有毒的。工廠把污水排進河裡時，這些化學物質會溶解並擴散，傷害魚類和整條河流的生態系。低價也建立在低薪之上。有些工廠工人工時很長、薪水卻很少，這引發了嚴重的道德問題。許多公司並不公開衣服是在哪裡、如何製造的，所以消費者很難查明。
問題在我們買下之後仍在持續。因為衣服太便宜，人們常買下遠超過需要的數量，這種過度消費製造出堆積如山的垃圾。我們把舊衣捐給慈善機構時會覺得很好，但慈善機構收到的捐贈遠多於他們賣得掉的數量，其餘的大多被運往其他國家、燒掉或直接丟棄。
儘管如此，改變的跡象已經出現。許多年輕消費者熱衷於購買二手衣、修補自己已有的衣服，或與朋友交換衣物。他們清楚區分「想要」與「真正需要」。穿得好看，並不是每週買新衣的人才有的專利。所以下次買襯衫之前，先問問自己：這件衣服我至少會穿三十次嗎？

questions.stem: What happens to many of the clothes that people give to charity?

questions.stem: Which of the following would the writer most likely agree with?

Fast fashion is good because everyone can afford it.
Donating clothes solves the problem of waste.
Shoppers should think carefully about how often they will wear something.

questions.evidence: So before you buy your next shirt, ask yourself: Will I wear this at least thirty times?

vocab.stem: The loud music from next door ______ my sleep, so I woke up several times during the night.
vocab.explain: 隔壁的大聲音樂「打斷、干擾」了睡眠，害我半夜醒來好幾次，故選 disrupted。donate（捐贈）、disclose（揭露）、dissolve（溶解）都無法和 sleep 搭配表達這個意思。

vocab.stem: Sugar ______ quickly in hot tea, but it takes longer in cold water.
vocab.explain: 糖在熱茶裡很快「溶解」，在冷水中則較慢，故選 dissolves。embrace（擁抱；欣然接受）、exclude（排除）、donate（捐贈）都需要受詞，文意也不通。

title: The Wave That Traveled the World
paragraphs: An [[immense|L5-0446]] wave rises over three small boats, its white tips reaching out like fingers. Far in the background, Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, looks tiny. This picture, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, was created by the Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai around 1831, when he was already in his seventies. Today it is an [[icon|L5-0442]] of Japanese art.

The Great Wave is not a painting but a woodblock print. Making it was a [[collaboration|L5-0153]]: Hokusai drew the design, and skilled workers carved it into blocks of wood, one block for each color. Because this method could produce thousands of copies, the prints were cheap enough for ordinary people to buy. Hokusai also used Prussian blue, a new color from Europe. The deep blue [[intensifies|L5-0481]] the feeling of danger and gives the sea its [[distinctive|L5-0304]] look.

The picture [[fascinates|L5-0379]] people because it is open to different [[interpretations|L5-0485]]. Hokusai [[depicts|L5-0272]] the moment just before the wave crashes down. Some see the wave as a symbol of nature's terrible power. Others notice that the men in the boats keep rowing together. Is the picture about fear or about courage? Hokusai never explained, and that may be part of its charm.

After Japan opened its ports to trade in the 1850s, prints like this reached Europe and [[fostered|L5-0393]] a strong interest in Japanese art. Vincent van Gogh praised Hokusai's waves in a letter to his brother. Only a small [[fraction|L5-0395]] of the early prints survive, and they are kept in museums and other [[institutions|L5-0476]] from Tokyo to New York. Meanwhile, [[graphic|L5-0414]] designers still borrow its bold lines, and the wave even appears on Japan's 1,000-yen note. A picture made nearly two hundred years ago has become part of the world's shared [[heritage|L5-0430]].
zh: 一道巨大的浪在三艘小船上方高高捲起，白色的浪尖像手指一樣伸展開來。遠方背景中，日本最高的山——富士山——看起來小小的。這幅畫名為〈神奈川沖浪裏〉，由日本藝術家葛飾北齋在 1831 年左右創作，當時他已經七十多歲。如今它是日本藝術的代表象徵。
〈神奈川沖浪裏〉不是一幅畫作，而是木刻版畫。它的製作是一場合作：北齋畫出圖樣，技藝純熟的工匠再把它刻在木版上，每種顏色各用一塊版。因為這種方法能印出成千上萬份，版畫便宜到一般百姓也買得起。北齋還使用了普魯士藍，一種從歐洲傳來的新顏料。深沉的藍色加強了危險的感覺，也讓海水呈現出獨特的樣貌。
這幅畫令人著迷，是因為它可以有不同的解讀。北齋描繪的是巨浪即將打下來前的那一刻。有些人把海浪看成大自然可怕力量的象徵；也有人注意到，船上的人們仍在齊心划槳。這幅畫講的是恐懼，還是勇氣？北齋從未說明，而這或許正是它的魅力所在。
日本在 1850 年代開放港口通商後，這類版畫傳到了歐洲，激發了人們對日本藝術的濃厚興趣。梵谷曾在寫給弟弟的信中讚美北齋筆下的浪。早期印製的版畫只有一小部分留存至今，收藏在從東京到紐約的博物館及其他機構中。同時，平面設計師至今仍借用它大膽的線條，這道浪甚至出現在日本的千元鈔票上。一幅將近兩百年前的作品，已經成為全世界共同的文化遺產。

glosses.zh: 普魯士藍（一種藍色顏料）

questions.stem: How was The Great Wave made?
options: Hokusai painted every copy by hand.
Artists in Europe copied it from an older painting.
It was painted on a large piece of cloth.
Hokusai drew the design, and other workers carved and printed it.
questions.explain: 第二段說這是一場合作：北齋畫出圖樣，工匠再把它刻在木版上印製，故選 (D)。(A) 文中說它是能大量印製的版畫，不是一張張手繪。
questions.evidence: Making it was a collaboration: Hokusai drew the design, and skilled workers carved it into blocks of wood, one block for each color.

questions.stem: Why could ordinary people afford Hokusai's prints?
options: Hokusai gave them away for free.
Many copies could be produced, so they were cheap.
They were printed on very thin paper.
questions.explain: 第二段說這種方法能印出成千上萬份，所以版畫便宜到一般百姓也買得起，故選 (C)。(D) 紙的厚薄文中並未提到。
questions.evidence: Because this method could produce thousands of copies, the prints were cheap enough for ordinary people to buy.

questions.stem: Why does the writer ask "Is the picture about fear or about courage?" in paragraph 3?
options: To show that the picture can be understood in more than one way
To prove that Hokusai was afraid of the sea

title: Storms from the Sun
paragraphs: On the morning of September 1, 1859, the British scientist Richard Carrington was studying the sun with a telescope when he saw something [[extraordinary|L5-0374]]: two bright spots of white light suddenly appeared on its surface and faded within minutes. Less than a day later, colorful lights filled the night sky over much of the world. They were seen as far south as the Caribbean, and in the Rocky Mountains, the light was so bright that some workers got up and began making breakfast, thinking morning had come.

Scientists now know that Carrington had seen a powerful [[blast|L5-0090]] on the sun. Such explosions throw [[immense|L5-0446]] clouds of gas into space at great speed. Only a small [[fraction|L5-0395]] of them head toward Earth, but when one does, it strikes the planet's magnetic field, a natural [[shield|L5-0782]] that protects us. This can [[intensify|L5-0481]] the northern and southern lights and push them far from the poles. Scientists call such events space weather.

In 1859, the main electric technology was the telegraph, which sent messages along wires. During the storm, telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed, and sparks flew from some machines. A few operators even found they could still send messages after they had [[disconnected|L5-0297]] their batteries, because the storm was creating electric currents in the wires.

Our world now depends far more on electricity. In March 1989, a much weaker storm caused a power failure in Quebec, Canada, leaving millions of people without electricity for about nine hours. A storm as strong as the one in 1859 could [[disrupt|L5-0301]] satellites, GPS, and power systems across [[extensive|L5-0370]] areas.

Fortunately, there is good news. Space agencies and research [[institutions|L5-0476]] keep watch on the sun, so they can often [[anticipate|L5-0046]] a storm a day or more before it arrives. With this warning, power companies can [[implement|L5-0448]] safety steps, such as [[altering|L5-0040]] how electricity flows through their systems, and satellite operators can protect their equipment. No one can stop the sun, but by staying [[cautious|L5-0123]], we can greatly reduce the [[hazard|L5-0426]] it poses.
zh: 1859 年 9 月 1 日早上，英國科學家理查・卡林頓正用望遠鏡觀察太陽，忽然看見一件非比尋常的事：太陽表面突然出現兩個明亮的白色光點，幾分鐘內就消失了。不到一天後，世界許多地方的夜空都布滿了彩色的光芒。遠在南方的加勒比海地區也看得到；在洛磯山脈，光線亮到有些工人起床開始做早餐，以為早晨已經到了。
科學家現在知道，卡林頓看到的是太陽上一次強大的爆發。這類爆發會把巨量的氣體雲高速拋向太空。其中只有一小部分會朝地球而來，但一旦如此，它就會撞上地球的磁場——一道保護我們的天然防護罩。這會使南北極光變得更強烈，並把極光推到離兩極很遠的地方。科學家把這類現象稱為「太空天氣」。
1859 年時，主要的電力科技是電報，靠電線傳送訊息。風暴期間，歐洲和北美各地的電報系統都故障了，有些機器還冒出火花。甚至有幾位電報員發現，他們把電池拆掉之後竟然還能發送訊息，因為風暴在電線中產生了電流。
如今我們的世界依賴電力的程度高出許多。1989 年 3 月，一場弱得多的風暴造成加拿大魁北克停電，數百萬人斷電約九小時。一場與 1859 年同樣強烈的風暴，可能會讓大範圍地區的衛星、GPS 和電力系統都受到干擾。
幸好，還是有好消息。太空機構和研究機構持續監測太陽，所以通常能在風暴到來的一天或更早之前預先料到。有了這樣的預警，電力公司就能實施安全措施，例如改變電力在系統中的流動方式；衛星營運者也能保護他們的設備。沒有人能阻止太陽，但只要保持謹慎，我們就能大大降低它帶來的危險。

The life and work of Richard Carrington

title: Making Way for Butterflies
paragraphs: Every spring, drivers on a highway in Yunlin County may see a surprising sight: hundreds of dark purple butterflies crossing the road. These are purple crow butterflies, and they are among the few butterflies in the world that migrate in huge groups.

In winter, the butterflies gather in warm, quiet valleys in southern Taiwan, such as those in Maolin, Kaohsiung. There, thousands of them hang together from trees, using [[minimal|L5-0540]] energy until the cold season ends. When spring comes, they fly north in search of fresh flowers, which provide the [[nutrition|L5-0575]] they need before laying eggs. Scientists are still studying the [[mechanism|L5-0530]] that guides them along the same route year after year, but the journey is [[partly|L5-0604]] shaped by mountains and wind.

Sadly, part of that route crosses a busy highway. Butterflies fly low over the road, and the [[odds|L5-0579]] of being hit by a fast car are high. After [[nonprofit|L5-0568]] groups and volunteers began counting the butterflies, the problem became clear. The government then put up tall nets along the road, which push the butterflies to fly higher. During the busiest days, one lane is even closed so the butterflies can pass safely. This was a [[milestone|L5-0538]] for [[conservation|L5-0206]] in Taiwan, and it has greatly reduced the [[likelihood|L5-0511]] of accidents.

Protecting the butterflies' winter [[habitat|L5-0424]] matters just as much. [[Likewise|L5-0512]], in North America, monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometers to spend the winter in the mountains of Mexico, and there has been a [[noticeable|L5-0570]] [[decline|L5-0261]] in their numbers as forests disappear. Small creatures, it seems, need big help to finish their long journeys.
zh: 每年春天，雲林縣某條公路上的駕駛人可能會看見令人驚訝的景象：成百上千隻深紫色的蝴蝶正在穿越道路。牠們是紫斑蝶，是全世界少數會成群大規模遷徙的蝴蝶之一。
冬天時，紫斑蝶聚集在台灣南部溫暖、平靜的山谷裡，例如高雄茂林。在那裡，成千上萬隻蝴蝶一起掛在樹上，用最少的能量度過寒冷的季節。春天來臨時，牠們往北飛，尋找新鮮的花朵，取得產卵前所需的營養。科學家仍在研究是什麼機制引導牠們年復一年沿著同一條路線飛行，但這段旅程有一部分是受山脈與風向影響而形成的。
遺憾的是，這條路線有一段橫越繁忙的公路。蝴蝶低飛越過路面，被高速行駛的車輛撞上的機率很高。非營利團體和志工開始計算蝴蝶數量之後，問題才變得清楚。政府於是沿著道路架起高網，迫使蝴蝶飛得更高。在蝴蝶最多的日子裡，甚至會封閉一條車道，讓蝴蝶安全通過。這是台灣保育的一個里程碑，也大大降低了蝴蝶遭撞的可能性。
保護蝴蝶的越冬棲地也同樣重要。同樣地，北美洲的帝王斑蝶會飛越數千公里，到墨西哥的山區過冬；隨著森林消失，牠們的數量明顯減少。看來，小小的生物需要很大的幫助，才能完成牠們漫長的旅程。

title: The Empty Frame in the Salon
paragraphs: At 8:30 on Monday morning, Iris Lin walked into the [[salon|L5-0751]] of the old Chang Family [[Mansion|L5-0522]], now a small city museum where she volunteered on weekends. She stopped. On the wall above the piano hung an empty frame. The museum's most valuable work, a painting of a girl reading by the light of a lamp, was gone.

The director, Ms. Wu, was pale. "The glass in the windows isn't [[shattered|L5-0778]]," she said. "The doors were locked, and the motion [[sensors|L5-0769]] didn't go off." The night guard, Mr. Ho, [[persisted|L5-0620]] in saying that nobody had come in. "I made my [[patrol|L5-0610]] every hour," he said. "Everything was quiet."

Iris studied the empty frame and went over the [[sequence|L5-0772]] of events in her head. The painting was famous for its [[realism|L5-0701]]; visitors often said the girl looked alive. Last Saturday, Iris had noticed a tiny [[rip|L5-0742]] near the [[rim|L5-0740]] of the [[canvas|L5-0116]], where a child had touched it. She had written a report and left it on the desk of the museum's repair expert, Ms. Chen. Then she remembered something else: the alarm system was always switched off on Sunday afternoons for cleaning.

Iris hurried to the repair room at the [[rear|L5-0703]] of the building. There, on a long table, lay the painting, safe and sound. Ms. Chen, a [[cautious|L5-0123]] woman, had read the report on Sunday and decided it was too [[risky|L5-0743]] to wait, so she had taken the painting down before the alarm was turned back on. She had sent Ms. Wu a message, but the director had not checked her phone all weekend. Ms. Wu laughed with relief, and by ten o'clock the museum had [[resumed|L5-0730]] its normal schedule.
zh: 週一早上八點半，林艾芮絲走進老張家大宅的會客廳。這座大宅如今是一間小小的市立博物館，她週末都在這裡當志工。她停下腳步。鋼琴上方的牆上，只掛著一個空畫框。館內最珍貴的作品——一幅描繪女孩在燈光下讀書的畫——不見了。
館長吳女士臉色蒼白。「窗戶的玻璃沒有被打破，」她說，「門都鎖著，動作感應器也沒有響。」夜班警衛何先生堅稱沒有人進來過。「我每個小時都巡邏一次，」他說，「一切都很安靜。」
艾芮絲仔細看著空畫框，在腦中把事情的經過依序想了一遍。這幅畫以寫實聞名，參觀者常說畫中的女孩彷彿活生生的。上週六，艾芮絲注意到畫布邊緣有一道小小的裂痕，是一個孩子碰到的地方。她寫了一份報告，放在館內修復專家陳女士的桌上。接著她又想起一件事：每週日下午，為了打掃，警報系統都會關閉。
艾芮絲趕到建築後方的修復室。那裡的長桌上，正躺著那幅畫，完好無缺。做事謹慎的陳女士週日讀了報告，認為等下去太冒險，就在警報重新啟動前把畫取了下來。她傳了訊息給吳館長，但館長整個週末都沒看手機。吳館長鬆了一口氣笑了出來，十點鐘時，博物館已恢復正常的作息。

questions.stem: Why did the director think the painting had been stolen?

vocab.explain: 花瓶從桌上掉下來「摔碎」成好幾百片，故選 shattered。resume（恢復）、persist（堅持）、recite（背誦）都無法接 into pieces 表示碎裂。

vocab.stem: Climbing that mountain alone in winter is too ______; you should go with an experienced guide.

title: A Student Tries the Fold-Flat Lunch Box
paragraphs: Product Review: The Fold-Flat Lunch Box | Rating: 4 out of 5 stars | Reviewed by Yi-chen, 17. I bought this lunch box last month because my old one took up too much space in my school bag. It is made of soft rubber with a hard plastic lid, and it [[supposedly|L5-0874]] folds down to just three centimeters thick. Here is my honest opinion after four weeks.

First, the [[highlights|L5-0431]]. The design is [[striking|L5-0856]]: it comes in bright colors, and my friends kept asking where I got it. Folding it is [[straightforward|L5-0851]]. You simply press the sides down, and it becomes as flat as a book. This makes [[storage|L5-0849]] easy; I can [[stack|L5-0835]] three of them in a kitchen drawer. The lid seals tightly, too. I once carried soup in it, and not a single drop came out.

Now for the problems. My mother cooked a [[spicy|L5-0825]] curry for my lunch one day, and it left an orange [[stain|L5-0836]] on the inside. I had to [[soak|L5-0801]] the box in hot water overnight to remove most of the color. Also, if you [[sniff|L5-0800]] the box after washing it, you may notice a [[subtle|L5-0865]] smell of rubber. It is not strong, but it bothered my younger [[sibling|L5-0788]], who borrowed it for a school trip. Finally, the soft walls have little [[structural|L5-0857]] strength, so never put heavy books on top of a full box.

All in all, I would [[recommend|L5-0709]] this lunch box to students who carry their lunch every day and have little space in their bags. Just avoid foods with strong colors. If you decide to [[purchase|L5-0681]] one, check the sizes carefully. The small one is cute, but it holds only a little rice. I will [[submit|L5-0860]] another review after three months.
zh: 產品評論：可摺疊扁平便當盒｜評分：五顆星中的四顆｜評論者：怡辰，17 歲。我上個月買了這個便當盒，因為我舊的那個在書包裡太占空間。它由軟橡膠製成，配上硬塑膠蓋，據說可以摺到只有三公分厚。以下是我使用四週後的真實心得。
首先是亮點。它的設計很搶眼：有好幾種鮮豔的顏色，朋友一直問我在哪裡買的。摺疊方式很簡單，只要把側邊往下壓，它就會變得像書一樣扁。這讓收納變得很容易，我可以在廚房抽屜裡疊放三個。蓋子也密封得很緊，我有一次用它裝湯，一滴都沒漏出來。
接下來是缺點。有一天媽媽幫我煮了辣咖哩當午餐，結果在盒子內側留下了橘色的污漬。我得把盒子泡在熱水裡一整晚，才把大部分的顏色去掉。此外，洗完後如果湊近聞，可能會聞到淡淡的橡膠味。味道不重，但借去校外教學的妹妹還是很介意。最後，軟軟的盒壁結構不太堅固，所以裝滿時千萬別把重的書壓在上面。
整體來說，我會推薦這個便當盒給每天帶午餐、書包空間又不大的學生。只要避免顏色太重的食物就好。如果決定購買，要仔細確認尺寸。小的那款很可愛，但只裝得下一點點飯。三個月後我會再發表一篇評論。

title: Why a Rainy Island Runs Short of Water
paragraphs: Taiwan receives more than two meters of rain a year, roughly two and a half times the world average. With such [[abundant|L5-0006]] rain, you might think the island could never run short of water. Yet water [[shortages|L5-0784]] are fairly common here. Why?

The answer lies in geography. Taiwan's mountains are high and steep, and its rivers are short. When heavy rain falls, most of the water rushes into the sea within a few days. Timing matters, too. Much of the rain comes during the plum rain season in May and June and during typhoons in summer and autumn, [[whereas|L5-0988]] in much of the island the months from November to April are dry. This [[variation|L5-0956]] makes Taiwan [[vulnerable|L5-0980]] to drought whenever the typhoons fail to come.

That is exactly what happened in 2021. After a year with almost no typhoons, Taiwan faced its worst drought in more than half a century. Water levels at Sun Moon Lake dropped so low that the dry lake bottom was [[uncovered|L5-0936]], and [[widespread|L5-0990]] limits on water use were put in place in cities such as Taichung. Farmers were also asked to stop growing rice in some areas, a hard choice for an island where [[agricultural|L5-0030]] use takes up most of the water.

[[Undoubtedly|L5-0943]], Taiwan cannot control the weather, but it can manage water better. Many old pipes leak, so replacing them is one [[viable|L5-0968]] solution. Another is to clean water from homes and factories and use it again, [[thereby|L5-0899]] saving fresh water for drinking. Buildings can also [[utilize|L5-0951]] rain collected on their roofs. Each family can help, too: fixing a dripping tap or taking shorter showers adds up. To [[sustain|L5-0879]] its people, farms, and [[wildlife|L5-0993]], Taiwan needs to treat every drop as [[crucial|L5-0245]].
zh: 台灣一年的降雨量超過兩公尺，大約是全球平均的二點五倍。雨量這麼豐沛，你可能會以為這座島永遠不會缺水。然而，台灣缺水的情況其實相當常見。為什麼呢？
答案在於地理環境。台灣的山又高又陡，河川很短。大雨落下時，大部分的雨水在幾天之內就奔流入海。時間分布也有影響。大部分的雨集中在五、六月的梅雨季，以及夏秋的颱風季；相較之下，島上許多地方從十一月到隔年四月都很乾燥。這種變化讓台灣只要颱風不來，就很容易發生乾旱。
2021 年正是如此。在幾乎沒有颱風的一年之後，台灣面臨了半個多世紀以來最嚴重的乾旱。日月潭的水位降得很低，乾涸的湖底都露了出來，台中等城市也普遍實施限水措施。部分地區的農民還被要求停種稻米。對一座農業用水占了大部分用水量的島嶼來說，這是很艱難的抉擇。
毫無疑問，台灣無法控制天氣，但可以把水管理得更好。許多老舊水管會漏水，所以汰換水管是一個可行的辦法。另一個辦法是把家庭和工廠用過的水淨化後再利用，藉此把乾淨的水留給人們飲用。建築物也可以利用屋頂收集到的雨水。每個家庭也能出一份力：修好滴水的水龍頭、縮短洗澡時間，點點滴滴都會累積。為了養活人民、農田和野生動物，台灣必須把每一滴水都視為關鍵。

title: Night Owls by Nature
paragraphs: It is midnight, and you are wide awake, even though you have school tomorrow. Your parents may say you are lazy. But science suggests that something else is going on. During the [[adolescent|L5-0022]] years, the body clock goes through a natural shift. Teenagers' brains begin to release melatonin, a chemical that makes us sleepy, later at night than children's or adults' brains do. As a result, falling asleep at ten o'clock can feel very hard. Many parents are not [[acquainted|L5-0015]] with this science.

This is not [[abnormal|L5-0001]]; it is a normal stage of growing up. The problem is that school still starts early. Doctors say teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, but many get far less. When the alarm rings at six, the [[abrupt|L5-0004]] end to deep sleep leaves them tired for hours.

Missing sleep night after night has [[adverse|L5-0024]] effects. Long-term lack of sleep can harm [[cognitive|L5-0150]] skills such as memory and attention, making it harder to learn. It can also affect mood and lead to [[fatigue|L5-0380]] that makes sports and even crossing the street more dangerous. In the short term, a single night of poor sleep may cause [[acute|L5-0018]] problems such as headaches and poor focus.

For these reasons, many doctors [[advocate|L5-0025]] later start times for high schools. In 2014, a major group of American children's doctors [[recommended|L5-0709]] that classes begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Some school [[administrators|L5-0021]] have listened, and studies found that their students slept longer. Students can help themselves, too. They can [[allocate|L5-0037]] time for homework earlier in the evening and keep bright screens away before bed, since screen light can [[disrupt|L5-0301]] sleep. Getting enough sleep is not a waste of time; it is an investment [[worthy|L5-1000]] of your attention.
zh: 已經半夜了，你卻還很清醒，即使明天要上學。爸媽可能會說你懶散，但科學顯示，背後另有原因。在青春期，身體的生理時鐘會自然地往後移。青少年的大腦開始分泌褪黑激素——一種讓人想睡的化學物質——的時間，比兒童或成人的大腦更晚。因此，要在十點入睡可能會感覺很困難。許多家長並不了解這項科學知識。
這並不異常，而是成長過程中正常的階段。問題在於學校還是很早就開始上課。醫生說青少年每晚需要八到十小時的睡眠，但很多人睡得少很多。鬧鐘在六點響起時，深層睡眠被突然打斷，會讓人好幾個小時都覺得很累。
一晚又一晚的睡眠不足會帶來不良的影響。長期缺乏睡眠會損害記憶力、專注力等認知能力，讓學習變得更困難。它也會影響情緒，並造成疲勞，讓運動、甚至過馬路都變得更危險。就短期而言，即使只睡不好一個晚上，也可能引起頭痛、無法專心等急性問題。
基於這些理由，許多醫生主張高中應延後上學時間。2014 年，美國一個重要的兒科醫師團體建議，上課時間不應早於上午八點半。有些學校的行政主管聽取了這個建議，而研究發現，那些學校的學生睡得更久了。學生也可以自己想辦法。他們可以把寫作業的時間分配在傍晚較早的時候，並在睡前讓明亮的螢幕遠離自己，因為螢幕的光可能干擾睡眠。睡飽不是浪費時間，而是一項值得你重視的投資。

title: Reading the Feelings Behind the Words
paragraphs: Your friend says, "I'm fine," but her voice is quiet and she will not look at you. Do you simply accept her words, or do you notice the [[subtle|L5-0865]] signs that something is wrong? The ability to recognize and manage feelings, both your own and other people's, is often called emotional intelligence. The idea became widely known in 1995, when the writer Daniel Goleman published a best-selling book about it. He argued that success in school, at work, and in friendships depends [[partly|L5-0604]] on these skills, not only on how smart a person is.

At the heart of emotional intelligence is empathy, the ability to see a situation from another person's [[perspective|L5-0622]] and share in what that person feels. Empathy is not the same as feeling sorry for someone. It means trying to understand why a classmate is angry or why a [[sibling|L5-0788]] has gone quiet, even when you would feel differently in the same situation.

Empathy can feel especially hard during the [[adolescent|L5-0022]] years. Researchers have found that the human brain keeps developing into the early twenties, and the areas that help control strong emotions are among the last to mature. As a result, teenagers can be [[prone|L5-0671]] to sudden changes in mood, and their [[sensitivity|L5-0768]] to what friends think is often high.

The good news is that empathy can grow with practice, and simple habits make a [[noticeable|L5-0570]] difference. Listen without interrupting. Instead of jumping in with advice, ask open questions such as "What happened?" If your friend [[persists|L5-0620]] in saying she is fine, respect that, but let her know you are there. Being [[straightforward|L5-0851]] about your own feelings helps, too; admitting that you feel [[vulnerable|L5-0980]] at times does not make you weak.

Caring deeply for others can put a [[strain|L5-0852]] on you. Taking time to rest is not selfish; it allows you to keep supporting the people you love. Emotional intelligence cannot solve every problem, but it will [[undoubtedly|L5-0943]] help us build stronger and kinder relationships, [[thereby|L5-0899]] making school and home happier places for everyone.
zh: 你的朋友說「我沒事」，但她的聲音很小，也不肯看你。你會直接接受她的話，還是會注意到那些顯示有什麼不對勁的細微跡象？辨識並管理情緒——包括你自己的和別人的——的能力，常被稱為「情緒智力」（EQ）。這個概念在 1995 年廣為人知，當時作家丹尼爾・高曼出版了一本相關的暢銷書。他主張，在學校、職場和友誼中能否成功，有一部分取決於這些能力，而不只是取決於一個人有多聰明。
情緒智力的核心是同理心：能從別人的觀點看事情，並分擔對方感受的能力。同理心不等於替別人感到難過。它的意思是試著了解同學為什麼生氣，或兄弟姊妹為什麼變得沉默，即使換作是你，在同樣的情況下會有不同的感受。
在青春期，同理心可能會顯得特別困難。研究人員發現，人類的大腦會持續發育到二十出頭，而幫助控制強烈情緒的區域，是最晚成熟的部分之一。因此，青少年容易情緒起伏不定，對朋友想法的敏感度也往往很高。
好消息是，同理心可以透過練習而成長，簡單的習慣就能帶來明顯的改變。聆聽時不要打斷對方。不要急著給建議，而是問一些開放式的問題，例如「發生什麼事了？」如果朋友堅持說自己沒事，就尊重她，但讓她知道你會陪在她身邊。坦白說出自己的感受也有幫助；承認自己有時候會感到脆弱，並不代表你軟弱。
深深關心別人可能會讓你承受壓力。花時間休息並不自私，它讓你能夠繼續支持你所愛的人。情緒智力無法解決所有問題，但它無疑能幫助我們建立更牢固、更友善的關係，進而讓學校和家成為每個人都更快樂的地方。

questions.explain: 第四段說如果朋友堅持說自己沒事，就尊重她，但讓她知道你會陪在她身邊，故選 (C)。(D) 作者建議不要急著給建議，而是先問開放式問題。

questions.stem: The phrase "put a strain on you" in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 下一句說花時間休息並不自私，可以讓你繼續支持別人，可見深深關心他人會讓人疲累、有壓力，put a strain on 指「給……帶來壓力」，故選 (B)。

vocab.stem: The school decided to ______ more money to the library so that it could buy new books.

vocab.stem: The bus came to an ______ stop, and several passengers almost fell over.
vocab.explain: 公車「突然」停下，好幾位乘客差點跌倒，come to an abrupt stop 是常見說法，故選 abrupt。allergic（過敏的）、administrative（行政的）、worthy（值得的）都不能形容停車的方式。

title: The Map in Grandpa's Attic
paragraphs: While cleaning out her grandfather's [[attic|L5-0067]] last summer, Mei found a large, old world map rolled up inside a box. She spread it out on the floor and stared at it in [[awe|L5-0073]]. Then something strange caught her eye: Greenland looked almost as big as Africa. At first, she [[attributed|L5-0069]] this to a simple mistake.

Her grandfather laughed when she showed him. "That map is not wrong," he [[asserted|L5-0060]]. "It just tells the truth in its own way." He explained that the map was based on a design by Gerardus Mercator, who lived in the 1500s. Because the Earth is round, no flat map can [[depict|L5-0272]] it perfectly. Mercator's map kept the shapes of coasts and the directions between places correct, which made it a great [[asset|L5-0062]] to sailors. A ship could follow a straight line on the map using a compass. The price was that lands near the North and South Poles appear much larger than they really are. In fact, Africa is about fourteen times the size of Greenland.

Mei's interest was [[aroused|L5-0054]]. She learned that people have always drawn maps to make sense of the world. Over the centuries, map makers [[amended|L5-0042]] their maps again and again as [[expeditions|L5-0364]] returned with new information. Today, satellites and computers [[assess|L5-0061]] distances with amazing accuracy, and the maps on our phones work [[alongside|L5-0039]] GPS to guide us down every street.

Mei asked whether the old map was valuable. Her grandfather smiled and said it was only a printed copy, not something that would sell at an [[auction|L5-0070]]. Still, she hung it on her bedroom wall. Every time she looks at Greenland, she remembers an important lesson: a map, like any story, is shaped by the [[perspective|L5-0622]] of the person who makes it.
zh: 去年夏天，梅在整理爺爺的閣樓時，發現一個箱子裡捲著一大張古老的世界地圖。她把地圖攤在地板上，看得肅然起敬。接著，一件怪事引起了她的注意：格陵蘭看起來幾乎跟非洲一樣大。起初，她以為這只是一個單純的錯誤。

她拿給爺爺看，爺爺笑了。「這張地圖沒有錯，」他堅定地說，「它只是用自己的方式說實話。」他解釋，這張地圖是根據 1500 年代的麥卡托所設計的畫法繪製的。因為地球是圓的，沒有任何平面地圖能完美地描繪它。麥卡托的地圖保留了海岸的形狀和各地之間正確的方位，這讓它成為水手的一大利器：船隻只要靠著羅盤，就能沿著地圖上的直線航行。代價是，靠近南北極的陸地看起來比實際大得多。事實上，非洲的面積大約是格陵蘭的十四倍。
梅的興趣被激發了。她得知人類一直透過繪製地圖來理解世界。幾百年來，隨著探險隊帶回新的資訊，製圖者一次又一次地修正地圖。如今，衛星和電腦能以驚人的精確度估算距離，手機上的地圖也搭配 GPS，帶領我們走過每一條街。
梅問爺爺這張舊地圖值不值錢。爺爺笑著說，那只是一份印刷的複製品，不是能拿去拍賣的東西。不過，她還是把它掛在臥室牆上。每次看到格陵蘭，她就會想起一個重要的道理：地圖就像任何故事一樣，會受到繪製者觀點的影響。

questions.stem: Why was Mercator's map useful to sailors?

It was small enough to carry easily.
It kept directions correct, so ships could follow straight lines.
It included the newest information from satellites.

questions.stem: What is true about the real sizes of Greenland and Africa?

Africa is about fourteen times as large as Greenland.

questions.evidence: In fact, Africa is about fourteen times the size of Greenland.

questions.stem: The word "amended" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 探險隊帶回新資訊後，製圖者一次又一次地 amended 地圖，可知是「修改、修正」地圖，故選 (C)。(D) 文中並未提到手抄。

title: The Bell on the Barren Hill
paragraphs: When Mei learned she would spend the summer with her grandmother in a small mountain village, she packed her [[belongings|L5-0081]] with a heavy heart. The village had no movie theater, and her phone could barely find a signal. On her first evening, she felt [[boredom|L5-0099]] settle over her like the thick fog rolling down the hill.

Grandma, however, had a plan. Every morning they climbed to a [[barren|L5-0078]] hill where almost nothing grew. "Fifty years ago, tea plants were [[abundant|L5-0006]] here," Grandma said. "When the young people left for the city, the fields were forgotten." Now a few [[residents|L5-0726]] were trying to bring the tea back. Mei helped them dig a narrow [[canal|L5-0115]] to carry water from a stream to the plants. On the second day she slipped and got a large [[bruise|L5-0107]] on her knee, but she went back the next morning.

In the evenings, Mei [[browsed|L5-0106]] through Grandma's old photo albums. One picture looked [[bizarre|L5-0089]]: villagers in paper masks dancing around a huge [[bronze|L5-0105]] bell. "That was our summer [[carnival|L5-0119]]," Grandma explained. "It was the most [[beloved|L5-0082]] event of the year, but it stopped when the village became too quiet." Mei had an idea. Everyone who had helped with the tea deserved a [[bonus|L5-0095]]: a night of music, food, and dancing.

With her new friends, Mei baked a [[batch|L5-0079]] of rice cakes every day for two weeks, and they bought paper for lanterns in [[bulk|L5-0108]]. Some people warned her, "[[Beware|L5-0085]] of the afternoon storms." But on the last Saturday of August, the sky was clear, and over a hundred people came. When the old bell rang again, Mei knew with [[certainty|L5-0127]] that she would return. The village was no longer just a [[destination|L5-0280]] on a map; it felt like home.
zh: 小美得知自己要到山上小村子的外婆家過暑假時，心情沉重地收拾了行李。村子裡沒有電影院，手機也幾乎收不到訊號。第一天傍晚，無聊的感覺就像從山坡滾滾而下的濃霧一樣，籠罩著她。
不過，外婆早有打算。每天早上，她們都會爬上一座幾乎寸草不生的荒山。「五十年前，這裡到處都是茶樹，」外婆說，「年輕人都到城市去以後，這些田就被遺忘了。」如今，幾位居民正努力讓茶園重新復甦。小美幫他們挖一條窄窄的水道，把溪水引到茶苗那裡。第二天她滑了一跤，膝蓋撞出一大片瘀青，但隔天早上她還是回去了。
晚上，小美翻看外婆的舊相簿。有一張照片在她看來很古怪：村民戴著紙面具，圍著一口巨大的青銅鐘跳舞。「那是我們的夏日嘉年華，」外婆解釋，「那曾是一年中大家最喜愛的活動，但村子變得太冷清後就停辦了。」小美有了一個點子：每個幫忙種茶的人都值得一份額外的獎勵──一個有音樂、美食和舞蹈的夜晚。
在新朋友的幫忙下，小美連續兩週每天烤一批米糕，大家也大量採購了做燈籠的紙。有些人提醒她：「要小心午後雷陣雨。」但八月的最後一個星期六，天空晴朗，來了一百多人。當那口老鐘再度響起時，小美非常確定自己會再回來。這個村子不再只是地圖上的一個目的地，而是像家一樣的地方。

vocab.explain: 考前要學生把「隨身物品」放在教室後面，只留鉛筆和橡皮擦，故選 belongings。carnivals（嘉年華）、celebrities（名人）、canals（運河）都不能被學生放在教室後面。

title: Why We Laugh Together
paragraphs: Think about the last time you laughed so hard that your stomach hurt. Chances are you were not alone. Scientists have found that people are far more likely to laugh with others than by themselves. Any [[comedian|L5-0159]] knows this: a joke that gets a big laugh in a crowded theater may get no reaction from someone alone at home.

Laughter is also [[contagious|L5-0212]]. When we hear someone laugh, the brain [[circuits|L5-0139]] that control our own face become active, preparing us to join in. This is why TV comedies have long used recorded laughter: even when viewers know it is fake, it can [[trigger|L5-0927]] real smiles. Most laughing does not follow jokes. In one well-known study, researchers listened to people talking in public places and found that only a small [[chunk|L5-0138]] of laughs came after anything funny. Most followed ordinary comments like "See you later!" Researchers often [[cite|L5-0140]] this as evidence that laughter is mainly a social signal.

Laughter may also be [[beneficial|L5-0083]] to our health. Some [[clinical|L5-0146]] programs now use group laughter to help patients with [[chronic|L5-0136]] pain, though doctors agree it should support, not replace, regular treatment. A good laugh can also bring [[clarity|L5-0143]]. When the [[chaos|L5-0129]] of homework and tests feels like too much, a few minutes of laughing with friends can help you think straight again.

Not every laugh is a happy one. People sometimes laugh when they are nervous, and a [[cluster|L5-0147]] of classmates laughing in a corner can make an outsider feel left out. Still, the research tells a [[coherent|L5-0151]] story: laughter is a tool humans use to build friendships. So the next time you and a friend burst out laughing at the same moment, it may not be a [[coincidence|L5-0152]]. Your brains may be working together, like singers in a [[choir|L5-0133]].
zh: 想想你上一次笑到肚子痛是什麼時候。你當時很可能不是一個人。科學家發現，人和別人在一起時笑出來的機率，遠高於獨處的時候。喜劇演員都很清楚這一點：一個在擠滿觀眾的劇場裡引起哄堂大笑的笑話，換成一個人在家看，可能毫無反應。

笑也會傳染。我們聽到別人笑的時候，大腦中控制自己臉部的神經迴路會活躍起來，讓我們準備跟著笑。這就是為什麼電視喜劇長久以來都會使用預錄的笑聲：即使觀眾知道那是假的，它還是能引發真正的微笑。大部分的笑其實不是跟在笑話後面。在一項知名的研究中，研究人員在公共場所聽人們聊天，發現只有一小部分的笑是出現在好笑的事情之後，多數是跟在「待會見！」這類平常的話後面。研究人員常引用這項發現，作為笑主要是一種社交訊號的證據。
笑也可能對健康有益。有些臨床計畫現在會用團體大笑來幫助慢性疼痛的病人，不過醫生們都同意，這只能輔助、不能取代正規治療。好好笑一場也能讓頭腦清楚。當作業和考試的混亂讓人喘不過氣時，和朋友一起笑個幾分鐘，能幫助你重新好好思考。
不是每一種笑都是開心的。人有時候會因為緊張而笑，而一群同學在角落裡笑成一團，也可能讓旁人覺得被排擠。不過，研究結果呈現出一個前後一致的說法：笑是人類用來建立友誼的工具。所以下次你和朋友在同一瞬間爆笑出來時，那可能不是巧合，你們的大腦或許正像合唱團的歌手一樣，在一起合作。

vocab.explain: 洗碗、倒垃圾都是「家事」，故選 chores。chords（和弦）、clauses（條款；子句）、coffins（棺材）都不是可以「做」的日常工作。

title: The Long Journey of a Phone
paragraphs: The phone in your pocket is small and [[compact|L5-0169]], but it has traveled a long way to reach you. A single phone contains dozens of [[components|L5-0184]], from the screen and camera to the battery and tiny chips. To make them, companies need metals such as gold, silver, and copper, dug from the ground around the world.

Before a new model reaches stores, designers [[conceive|L5-0193]] of its shape and features. The parts are then made in factories in different countries and put together in yet another. The work requires [[competent|L5-0178]] engineers, because even a little dust can ruin a chip. Many people find it hard to [[comprehend|L5-0186]] the [[massive|L5-0526]] amount of energy and water that goes into a device that fits in one hand. In fact, much of the pollution linked to a phone is created before it is ever turned on.

Then comes the part we know best: using it. Phones have become a common [[commodity|L5-0164]], and many people replace theirs every two or three years. A new model is often [[comparable|L5-0170]] to the old one in what it can do, yet clever advertising can [[conceal|L5-0191]] this fact. Sometimes an old phone stops being [[compatible|L5-0173]] with the latest software.

What happens at the end? Many old phones sit forgotten in drawers or end up in the trash. This is a problem, because some of the chemical [[compounds|L5-0185]] inside can be [[toxic|L5-0915]] if they leak into soil and water. Recycling allows valuable metals to be recovered and used again, and in some places, shops that sell phones must [[comply|L5-0183]] with rules about collecting old ones. Experts suggest a sensible [[compromise|L5-0189]]: keep your phone longer, repair it when you can, and [[donate|L5-0311]] or recycle it when you are done. A more [[sustainable|L5-0880]] phone is often the one you already have.
zh: 你口袋裡的手機又小又輕巧，但它可是經過了漫長的旅程才來到你手上。一支手機含有數十個零件，從螢幕、相機到電池和微小的晶片都有。為了製造這些零件，公司需要金、銀、銅等金屬，這些金屬是從世界各地的地底下挖出來的。
新機型上市之前，設計師要先構想它的外型和功能。接著，零件在不同國家的工廠製造，再運到另一個國家組裝。這項工作需要能幹的工程師，因為一點點灰塵就可能毀了一片晶片。許多人很難理解，一個單手就能拿的裝置背後竟耗費了大量的能源和水。事實上，跟手機有關的污染，很大一部分在它第一次開機前就已經產生了。
接下來是我們最熟悉的階段：使用。手機已經成為一種普通的商品，許多人每兩、三年就換一支。新機型實際能做的事往往和舊機差不多，但聰明的廣告可能把這個事實掩蓋起來。有時候，舊手機則是因為不再相容於最新的軟體而被汰換。
最後會怎麼樣呢？許多舊手機被遺忘在抽屜裡，或被丟進垃圾桶。這是個問題，因為手機裡的某些化合物如果滲進土壤和水中，可能有毒。回收能讓珍貴的金屬被重新取出、再次利用；在某些地方，賣手機的商店必須遵守回收舊手機的規定。專家建議一個合理的折衷做法：手機用久一點，能修就修，用完後捐出去或回收。最環保、最永續的手機，往往就是你手上已經有的那一支。

questions.evidence: much of the pollution linked to a phone is created before it is ever turned on

questions.evidence: some of the chemical compounds inside can be toxic if they leak into soil and water

questions.explain: 新機型能做的事和舊機差不多，但聰明的廣告會讓人看不出這一點，conceal 意思是「隱藏、掩蓋」，故選 (D) hide。(A) prove（證明）與廣告想達到的效果相反。

title: From Failed Wallpaper to Bubble Wrap
paragraphs: In 1957, two engineers in New Jersey, Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes, had a clever idea. They sealed two sheets of plastic together, trapping air bubbles between them, and planned to sell the result as a new kind of wallpaper. From the product's [[conception|L5-0194]], they held a strong [[conviction|L5-0226]] that people would love it. They were wrong. Hardly anyone wanted plastic bubbles on their walls.

Instead of giving up, the two men began to [[contemplate|L5-0214]] other uses for their [[innovation|L5-0469]]. They [[contended|L5-0217]] that the bubbles could help keep greenhouses warm, but few buyers agreed. They had already received a [[patent|L5-0608]] and started a small [[corporation|L5-0231]] to make the material, so they kept searching.

The answer came in 1960, when a large computer company was preparing to ship a new machine. Computers then were huge but fragile, and protecting them on the road was a [[core|L5-0229]] concern. After a [[consultation|L5-0210]] with the two inventors, the company decided to test the bubbles as a packing material. The machines arrived safely, and the [[conversion|L5-0223]] of a failed wallpaper into packing material was complete. Soon, other [[corporate|L5-0230]] customers were [[coordinating|L5-0227]] large orders, and bubble wrap became a common way to protect goods.

Since then, the product has continued to [[evolve|L5-0351]]. Some gardeners use it to protect plants from the cold, and some families cover windows with it to keep heat inside. Its most famous use, however, has nothing to do with protection: popping the bubbles. Many people find it relaxing, and there is even a Bubble Wrap Appreciation Day on the last Monday of January. It may seem like a [[contradiction|L5-0220]] that a product made for walls became loved for something so different, but its story shows that a failure is sometimes just an idea waiting for the right use.
zh: 1957 年，美國紐澤西州的兩位工程師艾佛瑞・菲爾汀和馬克・夏瓦納想到了一個巧妙的點子。他們把兩張塑膠片封在一起，在中間困住許多空氣泡泡，打算把成品當作一種新式壁紙來賣。從這項產品構想之初，他們就深信大家會喜歡它。結果他們錯了，幾乎沒有人想在牆上貼塑膠泡泡。
兩人沒有放棄，而是開始思考這項新發明的其他用途。他們主張這種泡泡可以幫助溫室保暖，但沒什麼買家認同。他們已經取得專利，也成立了一家小公司來生產這種材料，所以繼續尋找出路。
答案在 1960 年出現。當時一家大型電腦公司正準備運送一台新機器。那時的電腦體積龐大卻很容易損壞，運送途中如何保護它們是核心的考量。在和兩位發明者諮詢討論之後，這家公司決定試用這種泡泡作為包裝材料。機器安全送達，一款失敗的壁紙就這樣成功轉變為包裝材料。不久後，其他企業客戶也紛紛安排大量訂單，氣泡布成為保護貨物的常見方式。
從那時起，這項產品持續演變。有些園藝愛好者用它保護植物免受寒害，有些家庭則把它貼在窗戶上來保住室內的熱氣。不過，它最出名的用途和保護一點關係也沒有：捏破泡泡。許多人覺得這很紓壓，甚至還有一個「氣泡布感恩日」，訂在每年一月的最後一個星期一。一個為牆面設計的產品，竟因為截然不同的用途而受人喜愛，看似矛盾；但它的故事告訴我們，失敗有時只是一個還在等待正確用途的點子。

title: Behind the Zoo Fence
paragraphs: For many children, a trip to the zoo is their first chance to see a lion or an elephant up close. In front of a giraffe, they may feel a sense of [[awe|L5-0073]] that no picture book can give. Yet zoos have become more and more [[controversial|L5-0221]]. Some people see them as places of learning and protection, while others believe that keeping wild animals behind fences is wrong.

Supporters [[contend|L5-0217]] that modern zoos do important work. Many take part in breeding programs for animals whose numbers are falling in the wild. The Arabian oryx, for example, had disappeared from the wild by the 1970s, but animals raised in zoos were later returned to the deserts of the Middle East. Zoos also teach millions of visitors about [[wildlife|L5-0993]] and raise money for [[conservation|L5-0206]] projects. To supporters, this is the [[core|L5-0229]] purpose of a zoo.

Critics, however, point to the [[constraints|L5-0209]] that zoo life places on animals. An elephant that would walk many kilometers a day in the wild may spend its life in a space no bigger than a few soccer fields. [[Boredom|L5-0099]] can lead to strange behavior, such as walking in circles or shaking the head over and over, often signs of [[chronic|L5-0136]] stress. Critics also note that animals cannot give [[consent|L5-0205]] to being kept on display, and they argue that respecting an animal's [[autonomy|L5-0072]] means letting it make its own choices.

Many people find themselves somewhere in between. They feel [[compassion|L5-0171]] for animals kept in small spaces, but they also hold a strong [[conviction|L5-0226]] that endangered species must not be lost. For them, the answer may be a [[compromise|L5-0189]]: zoos that keep fewer kinds of animals, give them larger and more natural [[habitats|L5-0424]], and choose species whose [[biological|L5-0088]] needs can really be met.

Scientists continue to [[assess|L5-0061]] how well animals live in different zoos, and the results are mixed. As you [[contemplate|L5-0214]] your next visit, it may be worth asking not only what you will see, but also how the animals live after the visitors go home.
zh: 對許多孩子來說，去動物園是他們第一次有機會近距離看到獅子或大象。站在長頸鹿面前，他們可能會感受到圖畫書無法給予的敬畏之情。然而，動物園卻變得愈來愈具爭議性。有些人把動物園視為學習和保護動物的場所，有些人則認為把野生動物關在圍欄後面根本是錯的。
支持者主張，現代動物園做的是重要的工作。許多動物園參與繁殖計畫，幫助那些在野外數量逐漸減少的動物。舉例來說，阿拉伯羚羊在 1970 年代時已在野外消失，但後來在動物園中繁殖長大的個體被送回了中東的沙漠。動物園也教導數以百萬計的遊客認識野生動物，並為保育計畫募款。對支持者而言，這才是動物園的核心目的。
然而，批評者指出動物園生活對動物造成的種種限制。一頭在野外一天可能走好幾公里的大象，可能一輩子都待在不比幾座足球場大的空間裡。無聊可能導致奇怪的行為，例如不停繞圈走或一再搖頭，這些往往是長期壓力的徵兆。批評者也指出，動物無法同意自己被拿來展示，並主張尊重動物的自主權，就是讓牠自己做選擇。
許多人則處在兩者之間。他們同情被關在狹小空間裡的動物，但也深信瀕臨絕種的物種不能就此消失。對他們來說，答案也許是一種折衷：動物園飼養較少種類的動物，給牠們更大、更接近自然的棲息環境，並選擇生物需求真正能被滿足的物種。
科學家持續評估動物在不同動物園裡生活得如何，而結果好壞參半。當你考慮下一次去動物園時，也許值得問問自己：除了會看到什麼之外，遊客回家後，那些動物又過著什麼樣的生活。

title: Learning Science in a Second Language
paragraphs: Walk down the [[corridor|L5-0234]] of some high schools today, and you may hear science being taught in English and history in Chinese. These schools follow a bilingual [[curriculum|L5-0251]], in which students learn school subjects in two languages instead of studying a second language only in language class. The idea is popular, but it is not as simple as it sounds.

Supporters say this approach is [[beneficial|L5-0083]] in several ways. Some studies have found a [[correlation|L5-0232]] between growing up with two languages and certain [[cognitive|L5-0150]] skills, such as switching quickly from one task to another. However, a correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other, and scientists still disagree about how strong the effect is. Using a language to solve real problems may also [[boost|L5-0097]] students' confidence and give them a wider [[perspective|L5-0622]] on the world.

Bilingual teaching has its challenges, though. Teachers must explain difficult ideas clearly in a second language, and not every school has enough teachers who can do so. If students cannot follow the lessons, they may end up with a knowledge [[deficit|L5-0264]] in subjects like math or biology. Some parents also worry that the [[coverage|L5-0240]] of each subject will shrink, because classes move more slowly.

Sixteen-year-old Ting remembers feeling lost at first. "In my first chemistry class, I could barely speak, so I drew [[crude|L5-0246]] pictures to show my answers," she says. A school [[counselor|L5-0238]] encouraged her to keep a notebook of new terms, and her teachers stayed patient and [[courteous|L5-0239]] whenever she made mistakes. By the end of the year, she could give a [[decent|L5-0259]] presentation in English. Her story suggests that bilingual education works best when schools set clear [[criteria|L5-0244]] for success and give students the support they need. With that help, many students [[defy|L5-0265]] their own low expectations.
zh: 走在現今某些高中的走廊上，你可能會聽到自然課用英文上、歷史課用中文上。這些學校採用雙語課程，學生用兩種語言學習各科目，而不是只在語文課上學第二語言。這個想法很受歡迎，但並不像聽起來那麼簡單。
支持者說，這種做法有幾個好處。一些研究發現，從小接觸兩種語言長大和某些認知能力之間有關聯，例如能迅速從一件工作切換到另一件。不過，有關聯並不代表其中一個導致另一個，科學家對這個效果有多強仍有不同看法。用一種語言來解決真實的問題，也可能提升學生的自信，並讓他們以更寬廣的視野看世界。
不過，雙語教學也有它的挑戰。老師必須用第二語言把困難的概念講清楚，而不是每所學校都有足夠能做到這點的老師。如果學生跟不上課程，他們可能在數學或生物等科目上出現知識落差。也有些家長擔心，因為上課進度變慢，各科教到的內容會變少。
十六歲的婷婷還記得自己一開始很茫然。「在第一堂化學課，我幾乎說不出話，所以只好畫簡單粗略的圖來表達我的答案。」她說。學校的輔導老師鼓勵她準備一本筆記本記下新的專有名詞，而每當她犯錯時，老師們也始終很有耐心、很有禮貌。到了學年結束時，她已經能用英文做一場不錯的報告。她的故事說明，當學校訂出清楚的成功標準，並給學生需要的支持時，雙語教育的效果最好。有了這樣的幫助，許多學生都能突破自己原本不高的期待。

title: Pacific Youth Science Forum: Program Guide
paragraphs: Welcome to the 2027 Pacific Youth Science [[Forum|L5-0392]]! About 300 student [[delegates|L5-0266]] from twelve countries will spend two days at Sea View High School sharing ideas about science and the future. Every [[participant|L5-0602]] will receive a printed [[directory|L5-0294]] with the names, schools, and email addresses of all delegates, so you can keep in touch afterward.

Day 1 (July 10): The forum begins at 9:00 a.m. with an opening [[ceremony|L5-0126]] in the main hall and a welcome speech by Dr. Helen Lin, [[deputy|L5-0275]] director of the forum. From 10:00 to 12:00, a doctor will give a talk titled "Can Computers [[Diagnose|L5-0284]] Disease?" about how computers help hospitals find diseases earlier. In the afternoon class, "Saving a Language," students will record older speakers of a local [[dialect|L5-0286]] and learn why the number of speakers can [[diminish|L5-0292]] quickly when young people stop using it.

Day 2 (July 11): The morning debate, "The Robot [[Dilemma|L5-0290]]," asks whether robots should make choices that affect people's lives. Each school [[delegation|L5-0267]] will present its view. Speakers will be given time to think, so take a [[deliberate|L5-0268]], careful approach instead of rushing to answer. From 1:00 to 3:00 p.m., students will build a simple telescope with a lens 5 centimeters in [[diameter|L5-0287]]. If the weather allows, students will watch the night sky from the school roof from 7:00 to 9:00 p.m.

Please note: Phones must be switched to silent during all talks so that they do not [[distract|L5-0305]] speakers. Between talks, visit the [[booths|L5-0098]] in the gym, where science clubs show their projects. Lunch is provided on both days. Delegates who need [[accommodation|L5-0011]] should contact the front desk by June 30. Special thanks to our student volunteers for their [[devotion|L5-0283]] and hard work.
zh: 歡迎參加 2027 年太平洋青年科學論壇！來自十二個國家、約三百名學生代表將在海景高中共度兩天，分享關於科學與未來的想法。每位參加者都會拿到一本印好的名錄，上面有所有代表的姓名、學校和電子郵件地址，方便大家會後保持聯絡。
第一天（7 月 10 日）：論壇於上午九點在大禮堂以開幕典禮揭開序幕，並由論壇副主任林海倫博士致歡迎詞。十點到十二點，一位醫生將以「電腦能診斷疾病嗎？」為題演講，介紹電腦如何幫助醫院更早發現疾病。下午的課程「搶救一種語言」中，學生將錄下當地方言的年長使用者說話，並了解當年輕人不再使用某種方言時，它的使用人數為何會迅速減少。
第二天（7 月 11 日）：上午的辯論「機器人的兩難」要討論機器人是否應該做出影響人們生活的決定。每一所學校的代表團都將提出自己的看法。發言者會有時間思考，所以請採取審慎、仔細的態度，不要急著回答。下午一點到三點，學生將動手做一架鏡片直徑五公分的簡易望遠鏡。如果天氣允許，晚上七點到九點學生將在學校屋頂觀賞夜空。
請注意：所有演講進行時，手機必須切換成靜音，以免干擾講者。演講之間的空檔，歡迎到體育館參觀各攤位，各科學社團會在那裡展示他們的作品。兩天都提供午餐。需要住宿的代表請在 6 月 30 日前與服務台聯繫。特別感謝我們的學生志工們的投入與辛勞。

vocab.stem: After failing the exam for the third time, Kevin was filled with ______ and felt that he would never pass.
vocab.explain: 第三次考試失敗，覺得自己永遠考不過，心中充滿「絕望」，be filled with despair 是常見說法，故選 despair。dialect（方言）、diameter（直徑）、directory（名錄）都不是情緒。

title: Too Good to Throw Away
paragraphs: Every evening, bakeries around the world face the same question: what should they do with the bread that did not sell? Too often, the answer is the trash can. According to the United Nations, roughly one third of all the food produced on Earth is lost or wasted. This is not only a [[dreadful|L5-0316]] waste of money. It also has a serious [[ecological|L5-0319]] cost.

Growing food uses land, energy, and huge amounts of water, so throwing food away wastes all of these too. Throwing away one apple is the [[equivalent|L5-0340]] of pouring the water used to grow it down the drain. In places suffering from [[drought|L5-0318]], this is especially painful. When food [[decays|L5-0257]] in huge piles of garbage, it gives off gases that trap heat in the air. These [[emissions|L5-0327]] add to global warming.

Fortunately, people are finding creative solutions. In many cities, young [[entrepreneurs|L5-0333]] have set up websites that let shops sell food at low prices just before closing time. Food banks collect extra food from [[donors|L5-0313]] such as supermarkets and restaurants and give it to families in need; in some places, families must meet certain conditions to be [[eligible|L5-0324]] for this help. Some bakeries now keep extra [[dough|L5-0315]] in the freezer instead of baking too much each morning, so they bake only what they expect to sell.

Each of us can make a difference, too. A [[documentary|L5-0308]] can open your eyes to the problem, but daily habits matter more. Plan your meals, avoid buying [[excessive|L5-0355]] amounts, and remember that a "best before" date is about quality, not safety. Some people [[envision|L5-0335]] a future in which wasting food feels as wrong as throwing trash on the street. Every meal that is eaten instead of thrown away is a step toward a more [[sustainable|L5-0880]] world.
zh: 每天傍晚，世界各地的麵包店都面對同一個問題：沒賣完的麵包該怎麼辦？答案常常是垃圾桶。根據聯合國的資料，地球上生產的所有食物中，大約有三分之一遭到損耗或浪費。這不只是可怕的金錢浪費，也會造成嚴重的生態代價。
種植食物要用到土地、能源和大量的水，所以把食物丟掉，也等於浪費了這一切。丟掉一顆蘋果，就等於把種這顆蘋果用的水倒進水溝。在飽受乾旱之苦的地方，這尤其令人心痛。食物在大垃圾堆裡腐爛時，會釋放出把熱困在空氣中的氣體，這些排放物會加劇全球暖化。
幸好，人們正在想出有創意的解決方法。在許多城市，年輕的創業家架設網站，讓商店在打烊前以低價出售食物。食物銀行從超市、餐廳等捐贈者那裡收集多餘的食物，再送給有需要的家庭；在某些地方，家庭必須符合特定條件才有資格得到這項幫助。有些麵包店現在把多出來的麵團放進冷凍庫，而不是每天早上烤太多，這樣他們就只烤預期能賣掉的量。
我們每個人也都能有所貢獻。紀錄片能讓你看清這個問題，但日常習慣更重要。規劃好三餐、避免買過量的東西，並記得「最佳賞味期限」指的是品質，而不是安全。有些人想像著一個未來，在那裡浪費食物就像在街上亂丟垃圾一樣令人覺得不對。每一份被吃掉而不是被丟掉的餐點，都是朝更永續的世界邁進的一步。

Why the United Nations studies farming

title: The Restless Ground Beneath Us
paragraphs: The ground under your feet is always moving. Earth's outer [[layer|L5-0502]] is broken into huge pieces called plates, which slide slowly toward, away from, or past each other, moving only a few centimeters a year. Where plates meet, pressure builds up over time. When rocks suddenly break and move, the ground shakes in an earthquake. In some of these places, hot melted rock also rises to the surface and may [[erupt|L5-0343]] from a volcano.

This explains why earthquakes and volcanoes are not spread evenly around the world. Many occur around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, an area called the Ring of Fire. Taiwan lies where two plates meet, so small earthquakes are common here. Many tall buildings are designed with [[flexibility|L5-0386]] so they can bend rather than break. Japan, also on the Ring of Fire, is home to Mount Fuji. Its [[fabulous|L5-0376]] views attract millions of visitors, but it is not [[extinct|L5-0373]]: it last erupted in 1707, and scientists keep a close eye on it.

It is no [[exaggeration|L5-0352]] to say that a large volcano can change life for millions of people when it erupts. In 2010, ash from a volcano in Iceland [[disrupted|L5-0301]] air travel across Europe for days, because the tiny [[particles|L5-0603]] could damage aircraft engines.

Yet volcanoes also bring [[exceptional|L5-0354]] benefits. Soil near volcanoes is rich, so farms on their slopes can be very productive. Layers of rock from volcanoes can act as a natural [[filter|L5-0383]], cleaning rain as it sinks into the ground. In Iceland, people [[exploit|L5-0367]] the heat beneath their feet to [[generate|L5-0405]] electricity and warm their homes. In [[essence|L5-0345]], the same forces that shake the ground also shape the land we live on. Islands such as Hawaii were [[forged|L5-0390]] by volcanoes, and this almost [[eternal|L5-0347]] movement of the Earth continues today.
zh: 我們腳下的地面其實一直在移動。地球的外層碎裂成許多巨大的碎片，稱為「板塊」，它們彼此緩慢地靠近、遠離或錯開，每年只移動幾公分。在板塊交會的地方，壓力會隨著時間累積。當岩石突然斷裂、移動時，地面就會搖晃，形成地震。在其中一些地方，熾熱的熔岩也會上升到地表，可能從火山噴發出來。
這說明了為什麼地震和火山並不是平均分布在世界各地。它們有許多發生在太平洋周圍，這個區域被稱為「環太平洋火山帶」。台灣位在兩個板塊交會的地方，所以這裡常有小地震。許多高樓在設計時都考量了柔韌性，讓建築物能彎曲而不會斷裂。同樣位於環太平洋火山帶的日本有富士山。它絕美的景色吸引數以百萬計的遊客，但它並不是死火山：它上一次噴發是在 1707 年，科學家一直密切注意著它。
說一座大型火山噴發時能改變數百萬人的生活，一點也不誇張。2010 年，冰島一座火山噴出的火山灰讓歐洲的空中交通中斷了好幾天，因為那些微小的粒子可能損壞飛機引擎。
然而，火山也帶來非凡的好處。火山附近的土壤很肥沃，所以火山坡上的農田產量可能很高。火山岩層也能當作天然的過濾器，在雨水滲入地下時把它淨化。在冰島，人們利用腳底下的熱能來發電和替住家供暖。本質上，讓地面搖晃的力量，也塑造了我們居住的土地。像夏威夷這樣的島嶼就是由火山打造出來的，而地球這種幾乎永無止境的運動，至今仍在持續。

Because Taiwan is close to Iceland

questions.stem: The word "exploit" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 冰島人用腳底下的熱能來發電和供暖，exploit 在這裡指「利用、開發」自然資源，故選 (A) make use of。(C) keep away from（遠離）與「用來發電」的意思相反。

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

Earthquakes happen only in Taiwan and Japan.

The movement of Earth's plates causes earthquakes and volcanoes, which bring both dangers and benefits.
questions.explain: 全文說明板塊運動造成地震與火山，接著談火山的危害（火山灰影響飛航）與好處（肥沃土壤、過濾、地熱），主旨是板塊運動帶來的危險與益處，故選 (D)。(C) 肥沃土壤只是第四段的一個細節。

vocab.stem: Dinosaurs became ______ about 66 million years ago, so we can only learn about them from their bones.
