vocab.stem: After a year as an exchange student in Canada, Jenny spoke English with such ______ that people thought she had grown up there.
vocab.explain: 她英文說得非常「流利」，別人以為她在加拿大長大，speak with fluency 指說得流利，故選 fluency。fleet（艦隊）、filter（過濾器）、format（格式）放進句中都無法形容說英文的能力。

title: The Apprentice Who Waited
paragraphs: On her first morning at the Stone Bridge Inn, sixteen-year-old Yu-ting woke before the sun. The sky over the mountains was [[gloomy|L5-0411]], and cold rain was falling. She had come as an apprentice to [[Chef|L5-0132]] Gao, a quiet man famous for cooking fish and vegetables over an open [[grill|L5-0418]]. Yu-ting had [[dedicated|L5-0262]] years to preparing for this chance, but on that first day, she did not touch a single knife.

Instead, Chef Gao sent her to the back door, where a truck had just dropped off the week's [[freight|L5-0400]]: boxes of vegetables, bags of rice, and heavy sacks of salt. She had to [[haul|L5-0425]] everything into the kitchen by herself. Then she picked [[herbs|L5-0429]] in the garden behind the inn and washed them leaf by leaf. By evening, she was shaking with [[fatigue|L5-0380]]. In bed, she thought of the [[gorgeous|L5-0412]] dishes she had seen online and wondered when she would ever make one herself.

Weeks passed. Chef Gao spoke little, but Yu-ting slowly gained [[insight|L5-0473]] into his way of working. He never wasted any food, and he never raised his prices, even when guests drove for hours to eat at the inn. "[[Greed|L5-0416]] ruins good food," he often said. To him, patient and honest work was the most [[honorable|L5-0433]] path a cook could take.

One stormy night, the chef caught a bad cold just as every table was full. His face was [[grim|L5-0419]], but he nodded at Yu-ting. She [[gripped|L5-0420]] her knife and began. With no recipe to follow, she trusted her [[gut|L5-0423]], adding herbs the way she had watched him do a hundred times. When an old woman at the first table tasted the fish, she [[gasped|L5-0403]] and asked who had cooked it. From the kitchen door, Chef Gao smiled for the first time in weeks.
zh: 在石橋旅店的第一個早晨，十六歲的郁婷天還沒亮就醒了。山上的天空陰沉沉的，冷冷的雨不停落下。她來這裡拜高師傅為師當學徒；高師傅話不多，以在明火烤架上烤魚和蔬菜聞名。郁婷為了這個機會已經努力準備了好幾年，但第一天，她連一把刀都沒有碰到。
高師傅反而叫她到後門去，一輛貨車剛把這星期的貨送到：一箱箱蔬菜、一袋袋米，還有好幾大袋沉重的鹽。她得一個人把所有東西搬進廚房。接著，她到旅店後面的菜園摘香草，一片一片葉子地洗乾淨。到了傍晚，她累得全身發抖。躺在床上時，她想起在網路上看過的那些漂亮料理，不知道自己什麼時候才能親手做出一道。
幾個星期過去了。高師傅很少說話，但郁婷漸漸看懂了他做事的方式。他從不浪費任何食材，也從不漲價，即使客人開好幾個小時的車來這裡用餐也一樣。「貪心會毀了好菜。」他常這麼說。對他來說，耐心而誠實地工作，是一個廚師所能走的最光榮的路。
一個暴風雨的夜晚，正當每張桌子都坐滿客人時，高師傅得了重感冒。他臉色凝重，卻朝郁婷點了點頭。她握緊刀子，開始動手。沒有食譜可以照著做，她就相信自己的直覺，照著看他做過上百次的方式加入香草。第一桌一位老太太嚐了一口魚，驚訝得倒抽一口氣，問這道菜是誰做的。在廚房門口，高師傅露出了好幾個星期以來的第一個笑容。

She carried supplies and washed herbs.

title: Reading the Code of Life
paragraphs: Why do some people have curly hair while their brothers and sisters have straight hair? Why do certain diseases run in families? For centuries, people noticed that children look like their parents, but no one could explain exactly how [[traits|L5-0916]] were passed down. The answer came from [[genetics|L5-0408]], a science that is now part of almost every high school biology [[curriculum|L5-0251]].

In the 1850s and 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and carefully recorded their colors and shapes. He found that traits did not simply blend together. Instead, each plant [[inherited|L5-0463]] separate "factors" from its two parents, and these factors followed clear rules. Mendel published his results in 1866, but few scientists paid attention. Only in 1900, years after his death, did other researchers realize how [[exceptional|L5-0354]] his work was. Today we call his factors genes.

Genes are made of DNA, a long, thin chain shaped like a twisted ladder. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick described this shape, relying [[partly|L5-0604]] on an X-ray image made by Rosalind Franklin. In [[essence|L5-0345]], DNA is a set of instructions written in a four-letter code that tells the body how to build and run itself. After that, the [[frontier|L5-0401]] of the field moved forward quickly. By 2003, an international team had read most of the human [[genetic|L5-0407]] code.

This knowledge has changed medicine. Doctors can now [[diagnose|L5-0284]] some diseases by testing a patient's genes, sometimes even before any [[symptoms|L5-0883]] appear. New tools even make it possible to change genes, which raises serious [[ethical|L5-0349]] questions. Should parents be allowed to choose the traits of their future babies? Such [[dilemmas|L5-0290]] have no easy answers.

Still, it would be an [[exaggeration|L5-0352]] to say that genes decide everything. Studies of twins show a strong [[correlation|L5-0232]] between genes and height, yet identical twins can still differ in health, interests, and personality. Genes give us a [[framework|L5-0397]], but they are not our [[destiny|L5-0281]]. The food we eat and the choices we make every day still matter.
zh: 為什麼有些人是捲髮，他們的兄弟姊妹卻是直髮？為什麼某些疾病會在家族中代代出現？幾百年來，人們早就注意到孩子長得像父母，卻沒有人能確切說明特徵是怎麼傳下去的。答案來自遺傳學——如今幾乎每一份高中生物課程都包含這門科學。
在 1850 到 1860 年代，一位名叫孟德爾的修士種了數千株豌豆，並仔細記錄它們的顏色和形狀。他發現，特徵並不是單純地混合在一起。每株植物會分別從雙親那裡遺傳到不同的「因子」，而這些因子遵循清楚的規則。孟德爾在 1866 年發表了研究結果，卻很少有科學家注意。直到 1900 年，也就是他過世多年之後，其他研究者才明白他的研究有多麼傑出。今天，我們把他所說的因子稱為基因。
基因是由 DNA 構成的；DNA 是一條細長的鏈，形狀像一座扭轉的梯子。1953 年，華生與克里克描述了這個形狀，他們有一部分是依據羅莎琳・富蘭克林拍攝的一張 X 光影像。本質上，DNA 是一套用四個字母寫成的密碼指令，告訴身體如何建構與運作。在那之後，這個領域的研究前沿快速推進。到了 2003 年，一個國際團隊已經解讀了人類大部分的遺傳密碼。
這些知識改變了醫學。醫生現在可以透過檢測病人的基因來診斷某些疾病，有時甚至在任何症狀出現之前就能發現。新的技術甚至讓改變基因成為可能，這引發了嚴肅的倫理問題：父母應該被允許為未來的寶寶挑選特徵嗎？這樣的兩難沒有簡單的答案。
儘管如此，若說基因決定一切，那就太誇大了。雙胞胎研究顯示，基因和身高之間有很強的相關性；然而同卵雙胞胎在健康、興趣和個性上仍可能不同。基因給了我們一個基本架構，卻不是我們的命運。我們吃的食物和每天所做的選擇依然很重要。

title: Two Ways of Thinking
paragraphs: Every day, we make many decisions, from what to eat to which bus to take. Most of us believe we make them carefully. Psychologists, however, have shown that this is often an [[illusion|L5-0445]]. Daniel Kahneman, who won a Nobel Prize in 2002, described two systems of thinking. One is fast and acts on [[impulse|L5-0450]]; the other is slow and careful.

Fast thinking is [[indispensable|L5-0456]]. Without it, we could never catch a falling cup. But it also relies on quick rules of thumb, and these can lead to [[cognitive|L5-0150]] [[biases|L5-0086]]. Imagine a jacket whose price tag says $300, crossed out and replaced by $150. Many shoppers feel they are getting a great deal, even if the jacket was never worth $300. The first number sticks in the mind, and stores use such prices as an [[incentive|L5-0451]] to buy.

Our choices also depend on how they are presented. In some countries, people have to check a box if they want to become organ [[donors|L5-0313]]. In others, everyone is a donor unless they check a box to say no. Researchers have found that far more people become donors in the second kind of country. Since most people keep whatever has already been chosen for them, the design of a form can shape many lives.

Does this mean that poor decisions are [[inevitable|L5-0458]]? Not at all. The [[implication|L5-0449]] is that we should slow down when a choice really matters. Before a big [[purchase|L5-0681]], wait a day and think about your true [[intent|L5-0482]]: do you need this, or is it just exciting? In a world of almost [[infinite|L5-0460]] choices, we will never be completely [[indifferent|L5-0454]] to clever prices and ads. But if we [[incorporate|L5-0452]] a short pause into our habits, the slow, careful part of the mind gets a chance to speak.
zh: 每天，我們都要做許多決定，從吃什麼到搭哪一班公車都是。我們大多相信自己是經過仔細考慮才做決定的。然而，心理學家已經證明，這往往只是一種錯覺。2002 年獲得諾貝爾獎的丹尼爾・康納曼描述了兩種思考系統：一種快速、憑衝動行事；另一種則緩慢而謹慎。
快速思考是不可或缺的。沒有它，我們永遠接不住掉落的杯子。但它也依賴一些快速的經驗法則，而這些法則可能導致認知偏誤。想像一件夾克，標價寫著 300 美元，被劃掉後改成 150 美元。許多顧客會覺得自己撿到便宜，即使這件夾克從來就不值 300 美元。第一個數字會留在腦海裡，而商店就利用這種標價來刺激購買。
我們的選擇也取決於選項是如何呈現的。在某些國家，人們必須在表格上勾選，才會成為器官捐贈者；在另一些國家，除非勾選表示拒絕，否則每個人都是捐贈者。研究人員發現，第二類國家的捐贈者多出許多。由於大部分人都會維持已經替他們選好的選項，表格的設計就能影響許多人的人生。
這是否表示做出糟糕的決定是無法避免的？完全不是。這件事的意涵是：當選擇真正重要時，我們應該放慢腳步。在買大件東西之前，先等一天，想想自己真正的意圖：你是真的需要它，還是只是一時興奮？在一個選擇幾乎無窮無盡的世界裡，我們永遠不可能對巧妙的標價和廣告完全無動於衷。但如果我們在習慣中加入短暫的停頓，大腦中那個緩慢而謹慎的部分就有機會發聲。

title: Still Waiting for Hot Water
paragraphs:
Dear Mr. Lin,
I am writing as a [[resident|L5-0726]] of Apartment 5B at Green Hill Apartments to make a formal complaint about the water heater in my unit. It stopped working on March 3, and I reported the problem to your office that same day. More than five weeks later, it has still not been repaired.

Since then, my family has had to heat water on the stove and carry it to the bathroom in [[jugs|L5-0493]]. This is not only tiring but also a safety [[hazard|L5-0426]], especially for my young son. Your [[maintenance|L5-0517]] workers came twice, at an [[interval|L5-0486]] of about two weeks, but each time they said they had to order a new part. No one has contacted me since their second visit.

There is also a second problem. Water from the broken heater has leaked into the wall, and [[lumps|L5-0515]] of plaster are now falling from the ceiling of the shared [[lounge|L5-0514]] on the fourth floor. Several residents have stopped using the room as a [[precaution|L5-0645]]. The [[irony|L5-0489]] is that your website promises "worry-free living" to everyone who rents here.

I believe my complaint is [[legitimate|L5-0508]]. I have paid my rent on time every month, and I expect my [[landlord|L5-0498]] to keep the apartment in working order. I ask that the heater be repaired or replaced by April 20, [[lest|L5-0509]] the damage to the wall and ceiling become more serious. If I have not heard from you by then, I will have no choice but to ask the city [[housing|L5-0439]] office for [[intervention|L5-0487]]. I hope this will not be necessary, and I look forward to your reply.
Sincerely,
Hannah Wu
zh:
親愛的林先生：
我是綠丘公寓 5B 室的住戶，寫這封信是要正式投訴我家的熱水器。熱水器在 3 月 3 日壞掉，我當天就向您的辦公室通報了。如今已經過了五個多星期，它仍然沒有修好。
從那時起，我們家只能在爐子上燒水，再用水壺提到浴室。這不但很累人，也有安全上的風險，尤其對我年幼的兒子來說。你們的維修人員來過兩次，前後間隔大約兩週，但每次都說必須訂購新零件。自從他們第二次來過之後，就再也沒有人跟我聯絡。
另外還有第二個問題。壞掉的熱水器漏出的水已經滲進牆裡，四樓公共交誼廳的天花板現在有一塊塊灰泥剝落掉下。好幾位住戶為了安全起見，已經不再使用那個房間。諷刺的是，你們的網站還向每位房客保證「住得安心無憂」。

我相信我的投訴是合理正當的。我每個月都準時繳房租，也期待房東把公寓維持在正常可用的狀態。我請求在 4 月 20 日前修好或更換熱水器，以免牆壁和天花板的損壞更加嚴重。如果到那時仍未收到您的回覆，我將別無選擇，只能請市政府住宅單位介入處理。希望事情不必走到那一步，期待您的回覆。
敬上
吳漢娜

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the letter?
options: To ask the landlord for a lower rent
To complain about repairs that have not been made
To thank the maintenance workers for their help
To tell the landlord that the family is moving out
questions.explain: 第一段開頭就說明寫信是為了正式投訴熱水器的問題，後文也一再提到遲遲未修，故選 (B)。(A) 信中說她每月準時繳租，並沒有要求降租。

By heating water on the stove
By buying a new heater themselves

questions.evidence: I believe my complaint is legitimate. I have paid my rent on time every month

vocab.stem: After listening to all the evidence, the ______ decided that the man was not guilty.
vocab.explain: 聽完所有證據後判定被告無罪的是「陪審團」，故選 jury。jug（水壺）、laser（雷射）、lounge（交誼廳）都不能做出判決。

vocab.explain: 能精準對準、用來治療眼睛的細窄光束是「雷射」，故選 lasers。legacy（遺產）、league（聯盟）、lump（塊）都不是光束。

title: Can a Robot Really Care?
paragraphs: In the [[midst|L5-0536]] of a quiet afternoon at a care home in Japan, an elderly woman holds a soft white robot on her lap. It looks like a baby seal, a sea [[mammal|L5-0518]], and it moves its head and opens and closes its eyes when she speaks to it. It even makes gentle sounds in reply. For a few minutes, she seems calmer and happier.

Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world, and like many [[metropolitan|L5-0535]] areas elsewhere, its big cities do not have enough care workers. Robots are being tested to help fill this gap. Some remind patients to take their [[medication|L5-0531]] at the right time. Others help workers lift patients out of bed, which can [[minimize|L5-0541]] back injuries among staff. In the [[meantime|L5-0529]], robot pets like the seal are used for comfort. Studies suggest that this kind of [[therapy|L5-0898]] may be [[beneficial|L5-0083]] for patients who feel lonely or worried.

Not everyone welcomes these machines, however. Some people question the [[motive|L5-0553]] behind them: are care homes using robots to give better care, or simply to save money? Family members sometimes [[moan|L5-0544]] that a machine can never replace a kind word from a real person. There are also questions of [[morality|L5-0550]]. Is it honest to give a person with memory loss a machine that only seems to love her, especially when she is so [[vulnerable|L5-0980]]?

Most experts agree that robots should support human workers, not replace them. Designers now [[modify|L5-0547]] their machines based on advice from nurses, patients, and families. A helpful [[metaphor|L5-0534]] is a walking stick: it can support a person, but it cannot walk for her. The best care, many believe, will come when new technology and human care [[merge|L5-0533]].
zh: 在日本一家安養中心一個寧靜的午後，一位年長的女士把一隻柔軟的白色機器人抱在腿上。它看起來像一隻小海豹——一種海洋哺乳動物；當她對它說話時，它會轉動頭部、睜眼閉眼，甚至還會發出溫柔的聲音回應。有那麼幾分鐘，她看起來比較平靜，也比較開心。
日本是全世界人口最老化的國家之一，而且和其他地方許多大都會區一樣，日本的大城市缺乏足夠的照護人員。人們正在測試用機器人來填補這個缺口。有些機器人會提醒病人按時服藥；有些則協助照護人員把病人從床上抬起來，這樣能把工作人員背部受傷的情況減到最少。在此同時，像海豹這樣的機器寵物則被用來給人安慰。研究顯示，這類療法可能對感到孤單或焦慮的病人有益。
然而，並不是每個人都歡迎這些機器。有些人質疑背後的動機：安養中心用機器人，是為了提供更好的照護，還是只是為了省錢？家屬有時會抱怨，機器永遠取代不了真人的一句溫暖話語。這也牽涉到道德問題：給一位失智的人一台只是看起來愛她的機器，這樣誠實嗎？尤其她又是如此脆弱。
多數專家同意，機器人應該支援照護人員，而不是取代他們。設計者現在會根據護理師、病人和家屬的建議來修改機器。有個貼切的比喻是手杖：它能撐住一個人，卻不能替她走路。許多人相信，最好的照護會出現在新科技與人的關懷結合之時。

questions.stem: What does the robot in paragraph 1 look like?
questions.explain: 第一段說機器人看起來像一隻小海豹，故選 (A)。(D) 手杖是第四段用來說明機器人角色的比喻，並不是機器人的外形。
questions.evidence: It looks like a baby seal, a sea mammal

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, how do some robots help care workers?

They decide which medicine patients need.
They help lift patients out of bed.
questions.explain: 第二段說有些機器人協助照護人員把病人從床上抬起來，減少背部受傷，故選 (C)。(B) 機器人只是提醒病人按時吃藥，並不決定用什麼藥。

questions.stem: The word "moan" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 家屬 moan「機器永遠取代不了真人的一句溫暖話語」，這是表達不滿的話，可知 moan 指「抱怨」，故選 (D)。(B) 家屬是在質疑機器人，並不是表示贊同。

Japan has too many elderly people.
Robot pets are better than real pets.
questions.explain: 文章先介紹機器人在安養中心的用途，再提出動機與道德上的疑慮，最後說專家認為機器人應支援而非取代人力，故選 (B)。(A) 與最後一段的看法相反。

vocab.explain: 《蒙娜麗莎》被視為達文西最偉大的「傑作」，故選 masterpiece。mortgage（房貸）、molecule（分子）、missionary（傳教士）都不能指畫作。

vocab.stem: Every fall, millions of birds fly south in a long ______ to warmer places.
vocab.explain: 鳥群每年秋天往南飛到溫暖的地方，是「遷徙」，故選 migration。mandate（命令；授權）、massage（按摩）、mortality（死亡率）都不能描述鳥群飛行。

title: Making Room for the Rain
paragraphs: For a long time, the common [[notion|L5-0572]] was that cities could stop floods with higher walls and bigger pipes. Today, as storms grow heavier and summers hotter, many city planners believe this idea is [[naive|L5-0560]]. Rain has to go somewhere, and if there is [[nowhere|L5-0573]] for it to go, streets turn into rivers. Instead of only fighting nature, cities are learning to live with it.

Rotterdam, in the Netherlands, offers a well-known example. Much of the city lies below sea level, so flooding has always been a danger. In 2013, the city opened a "water square." On dry days, it is a public space where teenagers play basketball and friends sit and chat. During heavy rain, however, the square fills up and holds the water until the city's pipes can handle it. To most [[observers|L5-0578]], it looks like an ordinary playground, but it is also part of the city's [[infrastructure|L5-0461]].

Heat is the other danger. Concrete and roads take in heat from the sun and keep cities much warmer than the countryside. To cool things down, some cities are planting trees along streets and turning empty land into community [[orchards|L5-0588]]. Several [[municipal|L5-0556]] governments have gone further. Toronto, for instance, requires green roofs on many large new buildings, so plants on top of buildings are becoming the [[norm|L5-0569]] rather than an [[optional|L5-0587]] extra.

Such changes are not always easy. They cost money, and they can face [[opposition|L5-0584]] from [[residents|L5-0726]] who worry about taxes or losing parking spaces, so long [[negotiations|L5-0563]] are often needed. Still, many planners are full of [[optimism|L5-0586]]. They believe that cities have an [[obligation|L5-0576]] to protect the people who live in them, and that a greener, more [[sustainable|L5-0880]] city is also a more pleasant place to live.
zh: 長久以來，普遍的觀念是：城市可以用更高的牆和更粗的水管擋住洪水。如今，隨著暴雨愈來愈大、夏天愈來愈熱，許多都市規劃者認為這種想法太天真了。雨水總得流到某個地方，如果無處可去，街道就會變成河流。城市不再只是對抗自然，而是開始學習與自然共存。
荷蘭的鹿特丹就是一個有名的例子。這座城市有很大一部分低於海平面，因此淹水一直是個威脅。2013 年，市政府啟用了一座「水廣場」。天氣乾燥時，它是公共空間，青少年在這裡打籃球，朋友們坐著聊天。但下大雨時，廣場會積滿水，把水留住，直到城市的排水管能夠負荷為止。在大多數旁觀者眼中，它看起來就像普通的遊樂場，但它其實也是城市基礎建設的一部分。
高溫是另一個危險。混凝土和道路會吸收太陽的熱，讓城市比鄉下熱得多。為了降溫，有些城市在街道兩旁種樹，並把空地變成社區果園。有幾個市政府做得更多。例如多倫多規定許多大型新建築必須設置綠屋頂，因此在建築物頂上種植物正逐漸成為常態，而不是可有可無的附加設計。
這樣的改變並不總是容易的。它們需要花錢，也可能遭到擔心稅金增加或停車位減少的居民反對，因此常常需要長時間的協商。儘管如此，許多規劃者仍然充滿樂觀。他們相信，城市有義務保護住在其中的人，而一座更綠、更永續的城市，也是一個更宜居的地方。

options: How cities are adapting to floods and heat
Why Rotterdam is a popular place to visit
Why green roofs cost so much money

questions.explain: 規劃者認為「只靠高牆與粗水管擋洪水」的想法 naive，接著說明雨水若無處可去街道就會變河流，可知這個想法過於簡單、行不通，故選 (B)。(D) 這原本是普遍觀念，但 naive 本身並不是「受歡迎」的意思。

title: The Factory Boy Who Became a Writer
paragraphs: In 1824, a twelve-year-old boy in London was sent to work in a factory. Around the same time, his father was sent to prison because he could not pay his debts, and the family needed money. For about ten hours a day, he stuck labels onto jars of shoe polish in a dirty building by the river. This [[phase|L5-0626]] lasted only about a year, but he never forgot it. The boy's name was Charles Dickens.

Young Charles felt like an [[outsider|L5-0594]] among the other workers, and he was [[overwhelmed|L5-0600]] by shame. For most of his life, he kept this period a secret, telling only a close friend. The public learned about it only after his death, when that friend wrote the story of his life.

Yet those dark months shaped everything Dickens later wrote. Writing became an [[outlet|L5-0592]] for his feelings, and his novels [[depict|L5-0272]] the hard lives of poor children in great detail. In Oliver Twist, a hungry boy famously asks for more food. In David Copperfield, a young boy is sent to work in a dirty building near the river, much as Dickens himself had been. Readers have long noticed the clear [[parallels|L5-0601]] between this character's [[narrative|L5-0561]] and the writer's own childhood.

Dickens's [[output|L5-0593]] was huge: more than a dozen novels, along with many stories and articles. Critics have long praised the [[originality|L5-0590]] of his characters. He was also a [[passionate|L5-0605]] walker who often wandered the streets of London at night, watching the people he later wrote about. His stories show the cruel side of city life, but they are seldom filled with [[pessimism|L5-0623]]; kind hearts are often rewarded in the end. [[Overall|L5-0595]], his [[legacy|L5-0504]] is not only a shelf of great books but also a reminder that every child deserves a fair chance.
zh: 1824 年，倫敦一個十二歲的男孩被送進工廠做工。差不多同時，他的父親因為還不出債而被關進監獄，家裡需要錢。這個男孩每天工作大約十個小時，在河邊一棟骯髒的建築裡，把標籤貼到一罐罐鞋油上。這段時期只持續了大約一年，但他從來沒有忘記。這個男孩名叫查爾斯・狄更斯。
年少的查爾斯在其他工人之間覺得自己是個局外人，而且被羞恥感壓得喘不過氣。他一生大部分時間都把這段經歷當成祕密，只告訴過一位好友。直到他過世後，那位朋友寫下他的傳記，大眾才知道這件事。
然而，那段黑暗的日子影響了狄更斯日後寫的每一部作品。寫作成了他抒發情感的出口，他的小說細膩地描寫了窮苦孩子的艱難生活。在《孤雛淚》裡，一個飢餓的男孩說出了那句有名的「我還想再要一點」。在《塊肉餘生錄》裡，一個小男孩被送到河邊一棟骯髒的建築裡做工，就跟狄更斯自己當年一樣。讀者早就注意到，這個角色的故事和作者自己的童年有明顯的相似之處。
狄更斯的作品產量驚人：十幾部小說，再加上許多短篇故事和文章。評論家長久以來都讚揚他筆下人物的獨創性。他也是個熱愛走路的人，常在夜裡漫步倫敦街頭，觀察那些後來被他寫進書裡的人。他的故事呈現了城市生活殘酷的一面，卻很少充滿悲觀；善良的人最後往往會得到回報。整體來說，他留下的不只是一整排偉大的書，也是一個提醒：每個孩子都應該得到公平的機會。

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, who does "this character" refer to?

The young boy in David Copperfield

title: Voices of Taiwan's First Peoples
paragraphs: On a map of the Pacific Ocean, islands are spread from Hawaii to New Zealand. The people of many of these islands speak languages that belong to one large family, known as Austronesian. Where did this family begin? A widely accepted [[hypothesis|L5-0441]] points to Taiwan. Many experts believe that thousands of years ago, sailors from Taiwan began a long [[migration|L5-0537]] south and east, carrying their languages across the sea.

Today, Taiwan's government officially recognizes sixteen [[indigenous|L5-0455]] peoples, including the Amis, the Atayal, the Bunun, and the Tao. Each group has its own language and traditions, as well as [[myths|L5-0559]] about how the world and its first people came to be. For centuries, these stories were not written down but passed from elders to children by word of mouth, and each [[narrative|L5-0561]] carried lessons about nature, family, and respect.

Many traditions remain [[intact|L5-0477]]. On Orchid Island, the Tao build wooden boats by hand, fitting the boards together without metal nails, and they hold [[ceremonies|L5-0126]] to welcome the flying fish each spring. In the mountains, Bunun singers perform a prayer for a good millet harvest in which their voices rise slowly in rich harmony. When recordings of this song reached music experts abroad in the middle of the 1900s, many were [[astonished|L5-0064]] by its beauty.

However, the 1900s brought great changes. As Mandarin became the [[mainstream|L5-0516]] language in schools and on television, fewer young people grew up speaking the languages of their grandparents. Some languages are now spoken mainly by older people, and experts warn that their loss may be [[inevitable|L5-0458]] unless action is taken. In 2017, Taiwan passed [[legislation|L5-0506]] that recognizes indigenous languages as national languages and supports their teaching.

Many young indigenous people are now [[passionate|L5-0605]] about keeping their [[heritage|L5-0430]] alive. Some study their languages with elders; others [[incorporate|L5-0452]] traditional patterns and songs into fashion, pop music, and film with great [[originality|L5-0590]]. For them, culture is not something kept behind glass in a museum but a living [[legacy|L5-0504]] that each new generation can [[modify|L5-0547]] and pass on.
zh: 在太平洋的地圖上，島嶼從夏威夷一路分布到紐西蘭。許多島上的居民所說的語言都屬於同一個大語系，也就是南島語系。這個語系是從哪裡開始的？一個被廣泛接受的假說指向台灣。許多專家認為，數千年前，來自台灣的航海者開始往南、往東進行漫長的遷徙，把他們的語言帶過大海。
如今，台灣政府正式承認十六個原住民族，包括阿美族、泰雅族、布農族和達悟族。每個族群都有自己的語言和傳統，也有關於世界與最初的人類如何誕生的神話。幾百年來，這些故事並沒有被寫下來，而是由長輩口耳相傳給孩子，每一則故事都蘊含著關於自然、家庭與尊重的教誨。
許多傳統至今仍完整保存。在蘭嶼，達悟族人親手打造木船，不用金屬釘子就把木板接合在一起，每年春天還會舉行儀式迎接飛魚。在山區，布農族歌者會吟唱祈求小米豐收的祈禱歌，歌聲緩緩上升，形成豐富的和聲。二十世紀中期，這首歌的錄音傳到國外的音樂專家手中時，許多人都對它的美感到震驚。
然而，二十世紀也帶來了巨大的改變。隨著華語成為學校和電視上的主流語言，從小說祖父母那一代語言的年輕人愈來愈少。有些語言如今主要只有長者在說，專家警告，如果不採取行動，這些語言的消失可能無法避免。2017 年，台灣通過立法，承認原住民族語言為國家語言，並支持族語教學。
如今，許多年輕的原住民熱切地想讓自己的文化遺產延續下去。有些人跟著長輩學習族語；也有人把傳統圖紋和歌謠融入時尚、流行音樂和電影，展現極大的創意。對他們來說，文化不是放在博物館玻璃櫃裡的東西，而是活生生的傳承，每一個新世代都可以加以調整，再傳承下去。

title: The Plastic We Can't Pick Up
paragraphs: Early one Saturday, a group of high school students met at an old fishing [[pier|L5-0629]] for a beach litter [[pickup|L5-0628]]. By noon, they had filled twenty bags with bottles, plastic bags, and broken toys. Then their teacher asked them to [[poke|L5-0641]] through a handful of sand with a stick. Among the grains were tiny pieces of blue, red, and white. "These," she said, "are the plastics we can't pick up."

Scientists call plastic pieces smaller than five millimeters microplastics. Some are made small on purpose, but many come from larger objects that slowly break apart in the sun and waves. Others are [[fibers|L5-0382]] that come off our clothes in the washing machine, or tiny [[particles|L5-0603]] worn off car tires on the road. Because they are so small, they are very difficult to remove once they reach the sea.

Microplastics have now been found in almost every corner of the planet, from deep ocean floors to mountain snow and even drinking water. [[Preliminary|L5-0649]] studies have also found them in human blood. However, scientists say it is [[premature|L5-0650]] to conclude that they are making us sick. The [[premise|L5-0652]] that something must be harmful just because it is in our bodies needs careful testing. Medical [[practitioners|L5-0644]] still have many questions, such as whether certain plastics carry [[toxic|L5-0915]] chemicals into the body.

While research continues, many people are taking small steps. Some pay a [[premium|L5-0653]] for glass bottles, or use a water [[pitcher|L5-0633]] with a [[filter|L5-0383]] at home. Many cities and companies have made [[pledges|L5-0637]] to cut plastic waste. At the end of the beach day, the teacher's [[plea|L5-0635]] to her students was simple: "The best way to clean up plastic is not to throw it away in the first place."
zh: 某個星期六一大早，一群高中生在一座老舊的漁港碼頭集合，參加海灘撿垃圾活動。到了中午，他們已經裝滿了二十袋寶特瓶、塑膠袋和壞掉的玩具。接著，老師請他們用樹枝撥一撥一把沙子。在沙粒之間，有一些藍色、紅色和白色的小碎片。「這些，」她說，「就是我們撿不起來的塑膠。」
科學家把小於五毫米的塑膠碎片稱為塑膠微粒。有些是刻意做得很小的，但很多是較大的物品在陽光與海浪中慢慢碎裂而成。另外有些是我們的衣服在洗衣機裡脫落的纖維，或是汽車輪胎在路面上磨下來的微小顆粒。由於它們非常小，一旦進入海洋就很難清除。
如今，從深海海底到山上的積雪，甚至飲用水中，地球上幾乎每個角落都已發現塑膠微粒。初步研究也在人類的血液中發現了它們。不過，科學家表示，現在就斷定它們會讓我們生病還言之過早。「只要東西出現在我們體內就一定有害」這個前提，需要仔細驗證。醫療從業人員仍有許多疑問，例如某些塑膠是否會把有毒化學物質帶進人體。
在研究持續進行的同時，許多人正在採取一些小行動。有些人願意多花錢買玻璃瓶，或在家裡使用附濾心的濾水壺。許多城市和公司也承諾要減少塑膠垃圾。海灘活動結束時，老師對學生的懇切呼籲很簡單：「清理塑膠最好的方法，就是一開始就不要把它丟掉。」

title: What Coffee Does to Your Brain
paragraphs: According to a well-known legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia when a young man noticed that his goats became very lively after eating the red berries of a certain bush. True or not, people around the world now drink coffee every day, often [[prior|L5-0662]] to work or an exam. Many say it [[boosts|L5-0097]] their [[productivity|L5-0664]]. But what is it actually doing inside us?

The answer lies in caffeine. While you are awake, your brain slowly builds up a chemical called adenosine, which makes you feel sleepy. Caffeine has a similar shape, so it fits into the same places in the brain and blocks adenosine from doing its job. As a result, you feel more awake. Caffeine may also [[stimulate|L5-0845]] the heart, so your [[pulse|L5-0680]] may speed up a little, and in some people, too much of it can [[trigger|L5-0927]] feelings of worry.

The effects last longer than many people [[presume|L5-0659]]. For most adults, about half of the caffeine from a cup of coffee is still in the body five or six hours later. An afternoon coffee can therefore [[prolong|L5-0670]] the time it takes to fall asleep at night. People also react differently. In [[questionnaires|L5-0685]] about sleep, some say a late coffee has no effect on them, while others feel it for hours. Body size and genes [[presumably|L5-0658]] play a part.

Coffee has not always been welcome. In the 1500s, rulers in Mecca and some other places tried to [[prohibit|L5-0668]] it, in part because coffee houses had become popular places for people to gather and talk. Their efforts did not [[prevail|L5-0660]], and coffee kept spreading. Today, each type of bean has its own flavor [[profile|L5-0665]], and the drink has had a [[profound|L5-0666]] influence on daily life, from morning habits to the way people meet friends.
zh: 根據一個廣為流傳的傳說，咖啡是在衣索比亞被發現的：一位年輕人注意到，他的山羊吃了某種灌木的紅色果實後變得非常活潑。無論這個故事是真是假，如今全世界的人每天都喝咖啡，常常是在上班或考試之前。許多人說咖啡能提高他們的效率。但咖啡到底在我們體內做了什麼？
答案就在咖啡因。我們醒著的時候，大腦會慢慢累積一種叫做腺苷的化學物質，讓人覺得想睡。咖啡因的形狀和它很像，因此能卡進大腦中相同的位置，阻擋腺苷發揮作用。結果，你就會覺得比較清醒。咖啡因也可能刺激心臟，讓你的脈搏稍微加快；對某些人來說，攝取過多咖啡因還可能引發焦慮感。
咖啡的作用持續得比許多人以為的還久。對大多數成年人而言，一杯咖啡裡大約一半的咖啡因，在五、六個小時後仍留在體內。因此，下午喝一杯咖啡，可能會延長晚上入睡所需的時間。每個人的反應也不一樣。在關於睡眠的問卷中，有些人說晚上喝咖啡對他們沒有影響，有些人卻會感覺到好幾個小時。體型和基因大概都有影響。
咖啡並不是一直都受到歡迎。在 1500 年代，麥加和其他一些地方的統治者曾試圖禁止咖啡，部分原因是咖啡館已經成為人們聚集聊天的熱門場所。他們的努力並沒有成功，咖啡仍然持續傳播。如今，每一種咖啡豆都有自己的風味特色，而這種飲料也深深影響了日常生活，從早晨的習慣到人們和朋友見面的方式都是。

title: Four Weeks in New Zealand: Apply Now!
paragraphs: Have you ever dreamed of studying English somewhere far from home? This summer, the Global Classroom Program is [[recruiting|L5-0711]] high school students for a four-week stay in Auckland, New Zealand. Because the program has a [[quota|L5-0687]] of only twenty places, we encourage you to apply early.

On weekdays, you will take English classes in the morning. On the first day, everyone will take a short [[placement|L5-0634]] test so that each student can join a group at the right level. The student-teacher [[ratio|L5-0698]] is eight to one, so teachers can give each person plenty of attention. Afternoons are for exploring the city, and on the last weekend, everyone will spend two days on a sheep [[ranch|L5-0696]], where you can help feed the animals and learn about farm life. In the final week, each group will also perform a short play in English for the host families, so be ready for several [[rehearsals|L5-0715]]!

Many parents worry about safety. We would like to [[reassure|L5-0704]] them that every student will live with a carefully chosen host family, and our staff can be reached by phone 24 hours a day. The cost of the program covers classes, meals, and bike [[rental|L5-0720]], but not flights. Ten students from families in need will be the [[recipients|L5-0707]] of a full scholarship, and they will not have to [[repay|L5-0721]] any of the money.

To apply, fill out the online [[questionnaire|L5-0685]] and ask a teacher to write a letter of [[recommendation|L5-0710]]. No [[prior|L5-0662]] experience abroad is needed, just curiosity and an open mind. The deadline is April 30. A friendly [[reminder|L5-0717]]: if you do not have a passport yet, apply for one now, as it can take several weeks. This trip could open up a whole new [[realm|L5-0702]] of possibilities for you!
zh: 你曾夢想過到離家很遠的地方學英文嗎？今年夏天，「全球教室計畫」正在招募高中生，前往紐西蘭奧克蘭進行為期四週的遊學。由於本計畫名額只有二十個，我們鼓勵你及早報名。
平日上午你會上英文課。第一天每個人都要參加簡短的分班測驗，讓每位學生都能進入程度合適的班級。師生比是一比八，因此老師能給每個人充分的關注。下午是探索城市的時間；最後一個週末，大家會在一座綿羊牧場待兩天，你可以幫忙餵動物，認識農場生活。最後一週，每組還要為寄宿家庭演出一齣英文短劇，所以要準備好多次排練喔！
許多家長擔心安全問題。我們想讓家長們安心：每位學生都會住在經過仔細挑選的寄宿家庭，而且我們的工作人員二十四小時都能以電話聯繫。計畫費用包含課程、餐點和單車租借，但不含機票。十位來自經濟需要協助家庭的學生將獲得全額獎學金，而且不需要償還任何費用。
報名方式：填寫線上問卷，並請一位老師寫推薦信。不需要事先有出國經驗，只要有好奇心和開放的心胸。截止日期是四月三十日。貼心提醒：如果你還沒有護照，現在就去申請，因為辦理可能需要好幾週。這趟旅程可能為你開啟一個充滿可能性的全新天地！

title: More Than a Room Full of Books
paragraphs: When digital books and search engines became popular, many people predicted the end of public libraries. Why would anyone visit a building full of paper books when information was only a click away? To some, the idea of building new libraries even seemed [[ridiculous|L5-0737]]. Yet in many cities today, libraries are as busy as ever.

One reason is that libraries have changed. Instead of treating the Internet as a [[rival|L5-0745]], many have welcomed it. A typical library now offers free Internet access, computers, and online classes. Some hold [[seminars|L5-0765]] on how to spot fake news, while others help teenagers write [[scripts|L5-0762]] for short films. In one popular [[scheme|L5-0758]], young people teach older people how to use their phones, which [[reverses|L5-0733]] the usual roles of teacher and student.

Libraries also serve people who might otherwise be left behind. When libraries ask visitors why they come, many [[respondents|L5-0729]] say they come not only to borrow books but also to study, meet friends, or simply sit somewhere quiet and safe. For students whose homes are crowded, a library may be the only place to concentrate. In [[residential|L5-0727]] areas, it often becomes a meeting point for neighbors. [[Retail|L5-0731]] stores and coffee shops want visitors to spend money, but a library never does.

Imagine a [[scenario|L5-0756]] in which every library closed. Much information would still be available online, but people without computers or quiet rooms would lose a [[reservoir|L5-0724]] of knowledge and support. In the end, the belief that every town needs a library has [[prevailed|L5-0660]], and it is a [[rational|L5-0699]] belief. Libraries remain one of the few places where knowledge is free for everyone, and their effect on a community can be [[profound|L5-0666]].
zh: 當電子書和搜尋引擎開始流行時，許多人預言公共圖書館將走入歷史。資訊只要點一下就能取得，誰還會走進一棟滿是紙本書的建築呢？對某些人來說，興建新圖書館的想法甚至顯得荒謬。然而如今在許多城市，圖書館依然和過去一樣熱鬧。
原因之一是圖書館已經改變了。許多圖書館沒有把網路當成對手，反而張開雙臂迎接它。現在一般的圖書館會提供免費上網、電腦和線上課程。有些舉辦研討會，教大家如何辨識假新聞；有些則協助青少年撰寫短片劇本。在一項很受歡迎的計畫中，年輕人教長輩使用手機，這把一般師生的角色倒了過來。
圖書館也服務那些原本可能被拋在後頭的人。當圖書館詢問訪客為什麼來時，許多受訪者表示，他們不只是來借書，也來讀書、和朋友見面，或只是找個安靜又安全的地方坐坐。對家裡擁擠的學生而言，圖書館可能是唯一能專心的地方。在住宅區，圖書館常成為鄰居們聚會的地點。零售商店和咖啡店希望訪客花錢，圖書館卻從不如此。
想像一下所有圖書館都關閉的情境。許多資訊雖然仍能在網路上取得，但沒有電腦或安靜空間的人，將失去一座知識與支持的寶庫。最後，「每個城鎮都需要一座圖書館」的信念占了上風，而這是一個理性的信念。圖書館仍是少數人人都能免費取得知識的地方，它對一個社區的影響可能非常深遠。

title: Less Stuff, More Life
paragraphs: Open almost any closet, and you will probably find clothes that are rarely worn, shoes [[shoved|L5-0785]] into corners, and gifts still in their boxes. Modern life makes buying easy. Online stores never close, and [[retail|L5-0731]] ads follow us from one website to the next. During holiday sales, spending often [[soars|L5-0802]]. Before long, the [[sheer|L5-0780]] number of things we own can make our homes feel crowded and our minds feel tired.

In response, many people have turned to minimalism. Its basic [[premise|L5-0652]] is simple: owning fewer things can make life richer. Minimalists do not hate shopping, but they try to make [[rational|L5-0699]] choices instead of buying whatever catches their eye. Popular books and a [[series|L5-0773]] of TV shows have helped spread the idea, encouraging viewers to [[shed|L5-0779]] what they no longer need. This [[sentiment|L5-0770]] seems especially strong among young people who would rather spend money on experiences than on objects.

Letting go is not always easy, especially when objects have [[sentimental|L5-0771]] value. A ticket from a first concert or an old letter from a grandparent can hold strong feelings. To [[soften|L5-0805]] the pain of saying goodbye, many minimalists keep a few of these treasures and take photos of the rest.

Some critics [[shrug|L5-0786]] off the trend, saying that only people who already have plenty can choose to own less. That is a fair point. Still, the [[sole|L5-0806]] purpose of minimalism is not to live with almost nothing. It is to ask a simple question before buying: Will this really improve my life? For beginners, experts suggest setting aside a fifteen-minute [[slot|L5-0795]] each weekend to clear out one drawer or shelf. Each small step serves as a [[reminder|L5-0717]] that joy is not something we can carry home in a shopping bag.
zh: 打開幾乎任何一個衣櫃，你大概都會發現很少穿的衣服、被硬塞進角落的鞋子，還有連盒子都沒拆的禮物。現代生活讓購物變得很容易。網路商店從不打烊，零售廣告從一個網站跟著我們到下一個網站。在節慶特賣期間，消費往往暴增。沒多久，我們擁有的東西光是數量就足以讓家裡顯得擁擠，讓心也覺得疲累。
為了因應這種情況，許多人開始轉向極簡主義。它的基本前提很簡單：擁有較少的東西，能讓生活更豐富。極簡主義者並不討厭購物，但他們會試著做出理性的選擇，而不是看到什麼喜歡就買。一些暢銷書和一系列電視節目幫忙推廣了這個觀念，鼓勵觀眾丟掉不再需要的東西。這樣的想法在寧願把錢花在體驗而不是物品上的年輕人之間似乎特別強烈。
放手並不總是容易，尤其當物品具有情感價值的時候。第一場演唱會的票根，或祖父母寫的舊信，都可能承載著深厚的感情。為了減輕道別的痛苦，許多極簡主義者會留下少數幾件寶貝，其餘的則拍照留念。
有些評論者對這股潮流不以為然，認為只有本來就擁有很多的人，才有能力選擇擁有得少。這是個合理的看法。不過，極簡主義的唯一目的並不是過幾乎一無所有的生活，而是在購物前問自己一個簡單的問題：這真的能讓我的生活變得更好嗎？專家建議初學者每個週末空出十五分鐘的時段，清理一個抽屜或一層架子。每一小步都在提醒我們：快樂不是能裝進購物袋帶回家的東西。

title: Reading the Story in the Ice
paragraphs: High on mountain [[ridges|L5-0736]] and across the frozen lands near the poles, huge rivers of ice move so slowly that the human eye cannot see them travel. Glaciers form when snow falls year after year without melting. Under its own [[sheer|L5-0780]] weight, the old snow is pressed into solid ice. To scientists, glaciers are not just beautiful scenery but a library of Earth's past.

To read it, researchers drill into the ice and pull out long tubes called ice [[cores|L5-0229]]. Each section of a core matches a year or a [[series|L5-0773]] of years, and tiny bubbles trapped inside hold samples of ancient air. By studying these bubbles, scientists can learn what the air was like long [[prior|L5-0662]] to the age of factories. In Antarctica, cores have revealed the climate of the past 800,000 years, showing that cold and warm [[phases|L5-0626]] followed each other again and again.

Glaciers matter to the present as well. Together with the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, they hold the largest [[proportion|L5-0674]] of the world's fresh water. In Asia, mountain glaciers act as natural [[reservoirs|L5-0724]], slowly releasing water that feeds major rivers during the dry season. Their white surface also reflects much of the sun's [[radiation|L5-0690]] back into space.

Today, however, most glaciers are shrinking. As temperatures rise, they melt faster and [[shed|L5-0779]] huge blocks of ice into the sea. This creates a dangerous cycle: when the white ice disappears, the darker land or ocean below absorbs more heat, which leads to even more melting. [[Projections|L5-0669]] of future sea levels vary, but in the worst [[scenarios|L5-0756]], many cities by the sea could face serious floods. The [[prospect|L5-0676]] of losing glaciers also worries farmers who depend on mountain rivers.

Slowing the warming of the planet could [[prolong|L5-0670]] the life of many glaciers, though few scientists believe the damage can be completely [[reversed|L5-0733]] within our lifetimes. Standing at the edge of a glacier, many visitors feel a [[profound|L5-0666]] sense of time. Whether glaciers survive for future generations depends on the choices we make today.
zh: 在高高的山脊上，以及極地附近冰封的大地上，巨大的冰河移動得非常緩慢，人的肉眼根本看不出它們在前進。冰河形成的方式，是雪年復一年地落下卻沒有融化。舊雪在本身龐大的重量壓迫下，被壓成堅硬的冰。對科學家來說，冰河不只是美麗的風景，更是一座記錄地球過去的圖書館。
為了閱讀它，研究人員鑽進冰層，取出稱為「冰芯」的長管狀冰柱。冰芯的每一段都對應一年或連續好幾年，裡面困住的微小氣泡則保存著古代空氣的樣本。藉由研究這些氣泡，科學家能得知工業時代以前很久的空氣是什麼樣子。在南極洲，冰芯揭露了過去八十萬年的氣候，顯示寒冷與溫暖的階段一次又一次地交替出現。
冰河對現今的世界也很重要。冰河與格陵蘭、南極洲的巨大冰層加在一起，保存了全世界淡水中最大的比例。在亞洲，高山冰河就像天然的水庫，在乾季緩緩釋出水分，供給主要的河川。冰河白色的表面也會把大量的太陽輻射反射回太空。
然而如今，大多數冰河正在縮小。隨著氣溫上升，冰河融化得更快，並把巨大的冰塊崩落到海中。這形成了一個危險的循環：白色的冰消失後，底下顏色較深的陸地或海洋會吸收更多熱，導致冰融化得更多。對未來海平面的預測各不相同，但在最糟的情境下，許多海邊城市可能面臨嚴重的水災。失去冰河的可能前景，也讓仰賴高山河川的農民憂心忡忡。
減緩地球暖化可以延長許多冰河的壽命，但很少有科學家相信這些破壞能在我們有生之年完全逆轉。站在冰河邊緣，許多遊客會深刻地感受到時間的意義。冰河能否為後代子孫保存下來，取決於我們今天所做的選擇。

title: The Tiny Workers Behind Our Food
paragraphs: On a warm spring morning, a garden may seem quiet, but look closely and you will see bees moving busily from flower to flower. The [[sheer|L5-0780]] number of flowers a single bee visits in one day is surprising. As it collects food for its young, tiny grains of pollen stick to the hairs on its body and are carried to the next flower. This simple act allows plants to make seeds and fruit. Without it, many of the apples, berries, and [[squash|L5-0832]] we eat would never grow. Bees rarely sting unless you [[startle|L5-0840]] them.

Bees are also [[sophisticated|L5-0808]] travelers. They can see colors in the light [[spectrum|L5-0822]] that humans cannot see. Many flowers that look plain to us actually have [[spectacular|L5-0820]] patterns, visible only to bees, that guide them to the center. Honey bees even share information by dancing. When a bee finds good flowers, it returns home and performs a special dance that tells the others which direction to fly and how far to go.

In recent years, however, bee numbers in some places have [[plunged|L5-0638]]. Scientists [[speculate|L5-0823]] that several causes work together: chemicals used on farms, disease, the loss of wild flowers, and changing weather. Researchers collect [[specimens|L5-0819]] of sick bees to look for answers, but the full picture is not yet clear.

A great deal is at [[stake|L5-0837]]. Many farms depend on bees for their [[productivity|L5-0664]], and the [[stability|L5-0834]] of our food supply is closely tied to these tiny insects. The good news is that everyone can help. Families can [[sow|L5-0812]] wild flower seeds in their gardens, avoid chemicals that harm insects, and leave some corners of land a little wild. Some towns even [[sponsor|L5-0828]] programs that plant flowers along roads. Helping bees, after all, is a way of helping ourselves.
zh: 在溫暖的春天早晨，花園看似安靜，但仔細一看，你會發現蜜蜂正忙碌地在花朵間穿梭。一隻蜜蜂一天拜訪的花朵數量之多，令人驚訝。當牠為幼蜂採集食物時，細小的花粉粒會黏在牠身上的細毛上，被帶到下一朵花。這個簡單的動作讓植物得以結出種子和果實。少了它，我們吃的許多蘋果、莓果和南瓜類作物就永遠長不出來。除非你嚇到蜜蜂，否則牠們很少螫人。
蜜蜂也是精明老練的旅行者。牠們看得見光譜中人類看不到的顏色。許多在我們眼中平凡無奇的花朵，其實有著只有蜜蜂看得見的壯觀圖案，引導牠們找到花的中心。蜜蜂甚至會用跳舞來分享資訊。當一隻蜜蜂找到好的花叢，牠會回到巢中跳一種特別的舞，告訴其他蜜蜂該往哪個方向飛、要飛多遠。
然而近年來，有些地方的蜜蜂數量驟減。科學家推測是好幾個原因共同造成的：農場使用的化學藥劑、疾病、野花減少，以及不斷變化的天氣。研究人員收集生病蜜蜂的樣本來尋找答案，但完整的全貌仍不清楚。
這件事攸關重大。許多農場的生產力仰賴蜜蜂，我們糧食供應的穩定也和這些小昆蟲息息相關。好消息是，每個人都能幫上忙。家家戶戶可以在花園裡播撒野花種子、避免使用傷害昆蟲的化學藥劑，並讓土地的某些角落保持一點野性。有些城鎮甚至贊助沿著道路種花的計畫。畢竟，幫助蜜蜂就是幫助我們自己。

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what helps bees find the center of a flower?
options: The bright light of the sun
questions.explain: 第二段說許多花朵有只有蜜蜂看得見的壯觀圖案，引導牠們找到花的中心，故選 (B)。(C) 蜜蜂的舞蹈是告訴同伴往哪飛、飛多遠，不是找花的中心。
questions.evidence: Many flowers that look plain to us actually have spectacular patterns, visible only to bees, that guide them to the center.

questions.stem: What do scientists believe about the fall in bee numbers?
options: It is caused only by bad weather.
It has already been fully explained.
It happens only on large farms.
questions.explain: 第三段說科學家推測是好幾個原因共同造成的，故選 (C)。(A) 天氣只是原因之一；(B) 與「完整的全貌仍不清楚」矛盾。
questions.evidence: Scientists speculate that several causes work together

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, "A great deal is at stake" means that ______.
options: a lot of money is needed
a lot of work is finished
questions.explain: at stake 指「處於危險中、攸關重大」，接著作者說明農場的生產力和糧食供應的穩定都和蜜蜂有關，可見若蜜蜂消失我們會失去很多，故選 (A)。
questions.evidence: A great deal is at stake.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To teach readers how to keep bees at home
To explain why bees matter and how people can help them
To describe the history of honey
To warn readers that bees are dangerous
questions.explain: 文章先說明蜜蜂如何幫植物結果、牠們特別的能力，再談數量減少的問題，最後提出大家能做的事，目的在說明蜜蜂的重要與如何幫助牠們，故選 (B)。(D) 與第一段「蜜蜂很少螫人」的說法不符。
questions.evidence: Helping bees, after all, is a way of helping ourselves.

vocab.stem: In spring, the farmer ______ corn seeds in the field behind his house.
vocab.explain: 春天農夫在田裡「播種」玉米種子，故選 sowed。squashed（壓扁）、specified（具體說明）、startled（使嚇一跳）都不能與「在田裡」搭配，文意不通。

vocab.stem: The new study center is bright and ______, with plenty of room for fifty students.
vocab.explain: 「有足夠空間容納五十名學生」說明自修中心「寬敞」，故選 spacious。solo（單獨的）、squat（矮胖的）不適合形容房間；sophisticated（精密的；老練的）與「空間大」無關。

title: How to Break the Habit Loop
paragraphs: Why is it so easy to pick up your phone and so hard to pick up a textbook? Scientists often describe a habit as a [[loop|L5-0513]] with three parts. First comes a cue, a [[stimulus|L5-0846]] such as a sound, a place, or a feeling that tells the brain to act. Next comes the routine, the action itself. Finally, a reward makes the brain want to repeat the loop.

Because the reward arrives quickly, bad habits are hard to [[tackle|L5-0885]]. When your phone makes a sound, you are [[tempted|L5-0888]] to check it, and the small pleasure of a new message keeps the loop going. Simply trying hard to resist is rarely enough. Research suggests that people with good habits often do not fit the [[stereotype|L5-0843]] of having iron self-control; they simply arrange their surroundings well. A more [[strategic|L5-0855]] approach, then, is to change the loop itself.

Experts suggest several [[tactics|L5-0886]]. One is to remove the cue. If your phone stays in another room during a study [[session|L5-0775]], it cannot tempt you. Another is to [[swap|L5-0881]] the routine but keep the reward: if you eat snacks when you are bored, try taking a short walk instead. It also helps to [[specify|L5-0818]] exactly when and where you will act. "I will read at my desk after dinner" works better than "I will read more."

One well-known study found that forming a new habit took more than two months on average, though the time varied greatly. Missing a single day did not seem to cause [[substantial|L5-0863]] harm. If you skip your plan one day, do not give up; simply start again the next day. You do not need anyone to [[supervise|L5-0871]] you; a calendar on which you mark each success can be enough. With time and patience, the results can be [[superb|L5-0869]].
zh: 為什麼拿起手機這麼容易，拿起課本卻這麼難？科學家常把習慣描述成一個包含三個部分的循環。首先是提示，也就是一種刺激，例如一個聲音、一個地點或一種感覺，告訴大腦要採取行動。接著是慣性行為，也就是行動本身。最後，獎勵會讓大腦想再重複這個循環。
因為獎勵來得很快，壞習慣很難對付。手機一響，你就會忍不住想馬上查看，而收到新訊息的小小快感讓這個循環持續下去。光是努力克制通常不夠。研究顯示，擁有好習慣的人往往不符合「自制力超強」的刻板印象；他們只是把周遭環境安排得很好。因此，比較有策略的做法是改變這個循環本身。
專家建議了幾種策略。其一是移除提示。如果讀書時段手機放在另一個房間，它就誘惑不了你。其二是替換慣性行為但保留獎勵：如果你一無聊就吃零食，試著改成散步一下。具體說明你要在何時何地行動也很有幫助。「我晚餐後會在書桌前讀書」比「我要多讀書」更有效。
一項知名的研究發現，養成一個新習慣平均要花兩個多月，不過所需時間差異很大。偶爾漏掉一天似乎不會造成重大的影響。如果你某天沒照計畫做，別放棄，第二天重新開始就好。你不需要任何人監督；一本可以記下每次成功的月曆就足夠了。只要有時間和耐心，成果可以非常出色。

questions.stem: According to the passage, what are the three parts of a habit?
options: A cue, a routine, and a reward
A sound, a place, and a feeling
A plan, a calendar, and a success
A phone, a message, and a pleasure
questions.explain: 第一段說習慣是由提示（cue）、慣性行為（routine）和獎勵（reward）三部分組成的循環，故選 (A)。(B) 是「提示」的例子，不是習慣的三個部分。
questions.evidence: First comes a cue, a stimulus such as a sound, a place, or a feeling that tells the brain to act.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest for someone who eats snacks when bored?
options: Ask a friend to supervise them
questions.explain: 第三段說「替換慣性行為但保留獎勵」：無聊就吃零食的人，可以改成散步一下，故選 (B)。(A) 移除提示的例子是把手機放到另一個房間，不是零食。
questions.evidence: if you eat snacks when you are bored, try taking a short walk instead

questions.stem: The word "swap" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 作者建議 swap 慣性行為：把吃零食改成散步，也就是「替換」，故選 (C)。(A) 重複原本的行為正好與建議相反。
questions.evidence: Another is to swap the routine but keep the reward

questions.stem: What would the author most likely tell a student who missed one day of her reading plan?
options: She should give up and choose an easier habit.
She has lost all the progress she made.
She should study twice as long the next day.
She should simply continue the next day.
questions.explain: 第四段說偶爾漏掉一天似乎不會造成重大影響，與其放棄，不如第二天重新開始，故選 (D)。(B) 與「不會造成重大傷害」相反；(C) 文中沒有提到要加倍。
questions.evidence: do not give up; simply start again the next day

vocab.stem: We need a ______ table that can hold the heavy computer and printer.
vocab.explain: 要能放得下沉重的電腦和印表機，需要「堅固的」桌子，故選 sturdy。suburban（郊區的）、statistical（統計的）、supreme（最高的）都不能形容桌子的結構。

vocab.stem: The wires of my earphones are always in a ______ when I take them out of my bag.
vocab.explain: 耳機線從包包拿出來時總是「纏在一起」，in a tangle 表示糾結成一團，故選 tangle。surplus（過剩）、subsidy（補貼）、successor（繼任者）都與電線的狀態無關。

title: Where Do Great Ideas Come From?
paragraphs: For centuries, creativity was seen as a mysterious gift that only a few lucky people were born with. Thinkers could only [[speculate|L5-0823]] about where great ideas came from. Today, however, scientists can watch the brain at work, and the subject is moving from the [[theoretical|L5-0896]] to the practical.

One discovery is that new ideas often appear when the mind is relaxed. When you focus hard on a problem, certain parts of the brain keep your attention narrow. But when you take a walk, ride public [[transit|L5-0920]], or wait at an airport [[terminal|L5-0890]], another group of brain areas becomes more active. This network lets the mind wander and connect memories that normally stay apart. That may be why ideas often pop up during the quiet [[transition|L5-0921]] between sleep and waking.

Rest alone, however, is not enough. Studies suggest that creative people move back and forth between two [[modes|L5-0546]]: letting their minds wander and then judging which ideas are actually useful. Before a great idea arrives, they have usually spent long hours struggling with the problem. Some describe this stage as a [[torment|L5-0913]]. A student stuck on her [[thesis|L5-0900]] for weeks, for example, may find the missing piece while washing the dishes.

What does this mean for the rest of us? First, fight the [[temptation|L5-0889]] to fill every empty moment with your phone. Sitting in a quiet room with nothing but the [[tick|L5-0908]] of a clock may feel boring, but being bored can be a useful [[stimulus|L5-0846]]. Second, notice small things, such as the [[texture|L5-0893]] of a leaf; they give the brain fresh material. Creativity, then, is a [[substantial|L5-0863]] amount of hard work followed by rest. Understanding this can bring about a [[transformation|L5-0919]] in how we study: breaks are not wasted time but part of the process.
zh: 幾百年來，創造力被視為一種神祕的天賦，只有少數幸運的人天生就擁有。思想家們只能猜測好點子究竟從何而來。然而如今，科學家能觀察大腦運作的情形，這個主題也正從理論走向實際應用。
其中一項發現是：新點子常在心情放鬆時出現。當你專心解決一個問題時，大腦某些部位會讓你的注意力保持集中、範圍狹窄。但當你散步、搭乘大眾運輸，或在機場航廈等候時，另一組腦區會變得更活躍。這個網絡讓思緒四處漫遊，把平常分開存放的記憶連結起來。這或許就是為什麼點子常在半睡半醒之間那段安靜的過渡時刻冒出來。
不過，光是休息還不夠。研究顯示，有創意的人會在兩種模式間來回切換：先讓思緒漫遊，再判斷哪些點子真正有用。在好點子出現之前，他們通常已花了很長的時間苦思問題。有些人形容這個階段是一種折磨。舉例來說，一位卡在論文上好幾個星期的學生，可能在洗碗時找到了缺少的那一塊。
這對我們一般人有什麼意義呢？首先，抗拒用手機填滿每個空檔的誘惑。在一個只有時鐘滴答聲的安靜房間裡坐著可能很無聊，但無聊本身可以是一種有用的刺激。其次，留意小事物，例如一片葉子的質地；它們能給大腦新的素材。所以，創造力是大量的努力加上休息。了解這一點，能讓我們讀書的方式徹底轉變：休息不是浪費時間，而是過程的一部分。

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, when do new ideas often appear?
options: When we focus hard on a problem
When we are busy with homework
When we talk with other people
questions.explain: 第二段一開始就說新點子常在心情放鬆時出現，例如散步或等車時，故選 (B)。(A) 專心時注意力反而變得狹窄。
questions.evidence: One discovery is that new ideas often appear when the mind is relaxed.

questions.stem: What do creative people usually do, according to paragraph 3?
options: They rest all day and wait for ideas.
They avoid thinking about difficult problems.
They move between letting their minds wander and judging ideas.
They only work at airports and on trains.
questions.explain: 第三段說有創意的人會在讓思緒漫遊和判斷點子是否有用兩種模式間來回切換，故選 (C)。(A) 與「光是休息還不夠」矛盾。
questions.evidence: creative people move back and forth between two modes

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does "This network" refer to?
options: The group of brain areas that becomes more active when we relax
The parts of the brain that keep our attention narrow
The public transit system in a city
The memories that normally stay apart
questions.explain: This network 指前一句提到、在散步或等車時變得更活躍的「另一組腦區」，故選 (A)。(B) 是專心時運作的部位，正好是對照組；(D) 記憶是被這個網絡連結的對象。
questions.evidence: another group of brain areas becomes more active. This network lets the mind wander

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Only people born with a gift can be creative.
Phones are the main enemy of creativity.
Creativity comes from hard work combined with periods of rest.
Students should study without taking breaks.
questions.explain: 全文說明點子常在放鬆時出現，但在那之前要經過長時間的努力，最後總結創造力是大量努力加上休息，故選 (C)。(A) 是第一段提到的舊觀念；(D) 與結論相反。
questions.evidence: Creativity, then, is a substantial amount of hard work followed by rest.

vocab.stem: Our school's tennis team won first place in the national ______ last weekend.
vocab.explain: 網球隊在全國「錦標賽」中獲得第一名，故選 tournament。threshold（門檻）、treaty（條約）、theology（神學）都不是可以參加、得名的比賽。

vocab.stem: Two people who saw the accident agreed to ______ in court.
vocab.explain: 目擊車禍的兩人同意在法庭上「作證」，故選 testify。tick（打勾；滴答響）、thrust（猛推）、torment（折磨）放在 in court 前都不合文意。

title: Can a Machine Really Translate?
paragraphs: Not long ago, translation software often produced sentences that made readers laugh. Today, the picture is very different. Thanks to [[sophisticated|L5-0808]] programs trained on huge amounts of text, machine translation has improved at an [[unprecedented|L5-0947]] speed. A traveler can point a phone at a menu in Tokyo and read it in Chinese within seconds. For millions of people, such tools [[unlock|L5-0946]] information that was once out of reach.

Yet language is not only a set of words; it carries humor, culture, and feeling. Many [[verbal|L5-0961]] jokes depend on words that sound alike, and they often lose all their meaning in another language. Poems are even harder, since their sound and rhythm matter as much as their meaning. Some mistakes may seem [[trivial|L5-0930]], such as using a formal word in a friendly letter, but they can change the tone of a message. In a business contract or a medical report, a small error could [[undermine|L5-0940]] trust or even cause harm.

For this reason, many professional translators now work [[alongside|L5-0039]] machines. The software produces a first draft, and the human checks it, fixes errors, and adds the rich [[texture|L5-0893]] that makes writing feel natural. Their job has [[undergone|L5-0937]] a [[transformation|L5-0919]]: they spend less time writing every line and more time editing and judging. Because companies [[update|L5-0948]] and [[upgrade|L5-0949]] their programs all the time, translators must keep learning new tools.

Some people argue that learning foreign languages is no longer necessary. This idea is not entirely [[valid|L5-0954]]. Knowing another language lets you understand a culture from the inside and form friendships that no program can replace. Machines are useful tools, but they cannot [[undertake|L5-0941]] the whole task of understanding another person. The story of translation [[underlines|L5-0939]] a simple truth: communication is about more than words.
zh: 不久之前，翻譯軟體常常產生讓讀者捧腹大笑的句子。如今情況已大不相同。多虧以大量文字訓練而成的精密程式，機器翻譯以前所未有的速度進步。旅客在東京只要拿手機對準菜單，幾秒內就能讀到中文。對數以百萬計的人來說，這類工具解鎖了過去無法取得的資訊。
然而，語言不只是一組字詞；它承載著幽默、文化和情感。許多言語上的笑話建立在發音相近的字上，換成另一種語言往往就完全失去意義。詩更困難，因為詩的聲音和節奏跟意義一樣重要。有些錯誤看似微不足道，例如在親切的信中用了正式的字眼，卻可能改變訊息的語氣。在商業合約或醫療報告中，一個小錯誤就可能破壞信任，甚至造成傷害。
因此，如今許多專業譯者與機器一起工作。軟體先產出初稿，再由人來檢查、修正錯誤，並加上讓文字讀起來自然的豐富質感。他們的工作經歷了轉變：花在逐字逐句書寫的時間變少，花在編修與判斷的時間變多。由於公司不斷更新、升級程式，譯者必須持續學習新工具。
有些人主張學外語已經沒有必要。這個想法並不完全站得住腳。懂另一種語言，能讓你從內部理解一個文化，並建立任何程式都無法取代的友誼。機器是有用的工具，但無法承擔理解另一個人的全部任務。翻譯的故事凸顯了一個簡單的道理：溝通不只是文字而已。

questions.stem: What do many professional translators do today, according to paragraph 3?
options: They refuse to use translation software.
They check and improve drafts produced by machines.
They write programs for translation companies.
They translate only poems and jokes.
questions.explain: 第三段說軟體先產出初稿，再由人檢查、修正錯誤並讓文字更自然，故選 (B)。(A) 與「與機器一起工作」相反；(C) 文中說的是公司更新程式，不是譯者寫程式。
questions.evidence: The software produces a first draft, and the human checks it, fixes errors

questions.stem: Why are poems especially hard to translate?
options: Their sound and rhythm matter as much as their meaning.
They are written only in old languages.
Machines are not allowed to translate them.
questions.explain: 第二段說詩更難翻譯，因為詩的聲音和節奏跟意義一樣重要，故選 (B)。其他選項文中都沒有提到。
questions.evidence: Poems are even harder, since their sound and rhythm matter as much as their meaning.

questions.stem: The word "trivial" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 作者說有些錯誤看似 trivial，例如在親切的信中用了正式字眼，「但」可能改變語氣，可知 trivial 指「微不足道的」，故選 (C)。(A) 與文意相反。
questions.evidence: Some mistakes may seem trivial, such as using a formal word in a friendly letter

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's view of machine translation?
options: It is useful, but human understanding is still needed.
It will soon make human translators disappear.
It is too full of errors to be useful.
It is the best reason to stop learning languages.
questions.explain: 作者肯定機器翻譯的快速進步，但也指出語言中的幽默、文化與情感需要人來處理，最後說機器是有用的工具卻無法完全理解另一個人，故選 (A)。(D) 作者認為這個想法站不住腳。
questions.evidence: Machines are useful tools, but they cannot undertake the whole task of understanding another person.

vocab.stem: Besides ______, college students must pay for books, housing, and meals.
vocab.explain: 大學生除了「學費」之外，還要付書錢、住宿和餐費，故選 tuition。venue（場地）、trophy（獎盃）、tumor（腫瘤）都不是學生需要繳的費用。

vocab.stem: As the story ______, we learn that the quiet old man was once a famous piano player.
vocab.explain: 隨著故事「展開」，我們得知那位安靜的老人曾是知名鋼琴家，故選 unfolds。undo（解開；取消）、unlock（解鎖）、upgrade（升級）都需要受詞，也不能用來描述故事的進行。

title: Snow on the Windshield
paragraphs: The snow began just after lunch. By three o'clock, it was falling so heavily that Mei could hardly see the road through the [[windshield|L5-0994]]. Her father, a [[veteran|L5-0966]] driver who had made this trip to the mountain village every winter for twenty years, slowed the car down. "We'll be fine," he said, but Mei noticed that his eyes stayed [[wary|L5-0983]] and fixed on the road.

Mei had not wanted to come. She had planned to spend the holiday playing a [[virtual|L5-0973]] reality game with her friends, and for the first hour she had done nothing but [[whine|L5-0989]] about the poor phone signal. Now, as the trees grew darker and the road narrower, the silence felt [[weird|L5-0984]]. They were driving through real [[wilderness|L5-0992]], with no houses and no other cars in sight.

Then the car slid slowly into a pile of snow and stopped. The wheels turned, but the car would not move. They were [[stranded|L5-0853]]. Somewhere nearby, a branch broke with a loud crack that [[startled|L5-0840]] them both. Mei began to [[shiver|L5-0783]], partly from cold and partly from fear. Her father calmly called the village to report their [[whereabouts|L5-0987]], then took a [[sturdy|L5-0859]] shovel from the back of the car and began to dig. Without being asked, Mei put on her gloves and picked up a second shovel.

It took almost an hour. When the car finally rolled free, Mei was wet and tired, yet she felt strangely proud. Later that night, sitting by the fire in her grandmother's kitchen, she looked out at the mountains shining under the moon. The trip had been hard, but it had been [[worthwhile|L5-0999]]. She made a quiet [[vow|L5-0979]]: next time, she would complain less and help more.
zh: 雪在午餐後不久開始下。到了三點，雪下得又大又急，梅幾乎無法透過擋風玻璃看清道路。她的父親是開車的老手，二十年來每年冬天都走這趟前往山村的路。他把車速放慢，說：「我們不會有事的。」但梅注意到他的眼神依然謹慎，緊盯著路面。
梅本來不想來。她原本打算整個假期都和朋友玩虛擬實境遊戲，所以出發後的第一個小時，她什麼也沒做，只是一直抱怨手機訊號太差。此刻，樹林越來越暗，道路越來越窄，四周的寂靜讓人覺得怪怪的。他們正駛過一片真正的荒野，放眼望去沒有房子，也沒有其他車輛。
接著，車子慢慢滑進一堆積雪裡停住了。輪子空轉，車子卻動也不動。他們被困住了。附近某處一根樹枝啪的一聲斷裂，把兩人都嚇了一跳。梅開始發抖，一半因為寒冷，一半因為害怕。父親冷靜地打電話給村裡，報告他們的位置，接著從車後拿出一把堅固的鏟子開始挖雪。沒等人開口，梅就戴上手套，拿起了第二把鏟子。
這花了將近一個小時。當車子終於脫困向前滾動時，梅又濕又累，卻莫名地感到自豪。那天深夜，她坐在奶奶家廚房的爐火旁，望著窗外在月光下閃閃發亮的群山。這趟旅程很辛苦，但很值得。她在心裡默默發誓：下一次，她要少抱怨、多幫忙。

questions.stem: Why had Mei not wanted to make the trip?
options: She was afraid of driving in the snow.
She did not like her grandmother's village.
She had to finish her homework.
She had planned to play a game with her friends.
questions.explain: 第二段說梅原本打算整個假期和朋友玩虛擬實境遊戲，所以不想來，故選 (D)。(A) 她的害怕是後來車子卡住時才出現的。
questions.evidence: She had planned to spend the holiday playing a virtual reality game with her friends

questions.stem: What did Mei's father do after the car got stuck?
options: He walked to the village for help.
He waited in the car for the snow to stop.
He called the village and began to dig.
He asked Mei to push the car.
questions.explain: 第三段說父親冷靜地打電話給村裡報告位置，接著拿出鏟子開始挖雪，故選 (C)。(D) 文中說梅是主動幫忙，沒有人要求她。
questions.evidence: Her father calmly called the village to report their whereabouts, then took a sturdy shovel from the back of the car and began to dig.

questions.stem: The word "whereabouts" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 父親打電話給村裡報告他們的 whereabouts，好讓村民知道他們在哪裡，可知 whereabouts 指「所在位置」，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: called the village to report their whereabouts

questions.stem: How did Mei change during the trip?
options: She went from complaining to helping willingly.
She became more interested in online games.
She decided never to visit the mountains again.
She became afraid of her father.
questions.explain: 梅一開始只會抱怨，車子卡住後卻主動拿起鏟子幫忙，最後還發誓下次要少抱怨、多幫忙，可見她從抱怨轉為主動幫忙，故選 (A)。(C) 與「這趟旅程很值得」相反。
questions.evidence: She made a quiet vow: next time, she would complain less and help more.

vocab.stem: Thanks to the warm and sunny weather, the apple trees ______ more fruit this year than last year.
vocab.explain: 天氣溫暖晴朗，蘋果樹今年「結出」更多果實，yield 有「產出」的意思，故選 yielded。withered（枯萎）不接受詞且與好天氣矛盾；vowed（發誓）、worshiped（崇拜）都不合文意。

vocab.stem: Before the products are sent to stores, they are kept in a huge ______ near the port.
vocab.explain: 商品送到商店之前，先存放在港口附近的大「倉庫」，故選 warehouse。voucher（禮券）、verdict（判決）、volcano（火山）都不是存放商品的地方。

title: The Woman Who Kept Climbing
paragraphs: In the early 1970s, mountain climbing was widely seen as a man's sport. Many people believed the [[stereotype|L5-0843]] that women were too weak for the highest peaks. Junko Tabei of Japan was determined to prove them wrong. Her journey to the top of Mount Everest is a story of courage, patience, and a refusal to give up.

Tabei fell in love with climbing at ten, on a school trip to a mountain. As an adult, she often faced [[prejudice|L5-0648]]. Some male climbers refused to climb with her, and others said she should stay at home. Instead, in 1969 she started a climbing club for women. When the club decided to [[undertake|L5-0941]] an [[expedition|L5-0364]] to Everest, it was extremely hard to find a [[sponsor|L5-0828]]; many companies were [[wary|L5-0983]] of supporting women in such a dangerous activity.

The climb itself was a [[torment|L5-0913]]. The route included almost [[vertical|L5-0965]] walls of ice. In early May 1975, an avalanche buried Tabei and several team members while they slept at a camp. Although she was hurt, she [[vowed|L5-0979]] to continue. Twelve days later, on May 16, she reached the summit, becoming the first woman ever to do so. The achievement was [[unprecedented|L5-0947]], and it began a [[transformation|L5-0919]] in how the world saw women climbers.

By 1992, she had become the first woman to climb the highest mountain on each of the seven continents. As a [[veteran|L5-0966]] climber, she also grew worried about the garbage visitors left on Everest. She returned to university, wrote a [[thesis|L5-0900]] on the problem, and spent years working to protect the mountain [[wilderness|L5-0992]] she loved.

Her story [[underlines|L5-0939]] a simple truth: a summit is reached one step at a time. On a clear night high in the mountains, the stars look [[spectacular|L5-0820]], almost close enough to touch. Yet even from the highest peak, the sky still rises far above. For anyone working toward a difficult goal, that view carries a message: every summit is also a new starting point. The climb is hard, but it is always [[worthwhile|L5-0999]].
zh: 在 1970 年代初期，登山普遍被視為男人的運動。許多人相信一種刻板印象：女性太柔弱，無法攀登最高的山峰。日本的田部井淳子下定決心要證明他們錯了。她登上聖母峰頂的旅程，是一個關於勇氣、耐心與拒絕放棄的故事。
田部井十歲時在一次學校登山旅行中愛上了登山。成年後，她經常面對偏見。有些男性登山者拒絕和她一起爬山，也有人說她應該待在家裡。她沒有因此退縮，反而在 1969 年創立了一個女子登山社。當社團決定挑戰攀登聖母峰時，要找到贊助者極為困難；許多公司對於支持女性從事如此危險的活動抱持戒心。
攀登本身是一場折磨。路線中有幾乎垂直的冰壁。1975 年五月初，田部井和幾名隊友在山上的營地睡覺時，被雪崩掩埋。雖然她受了傷，仍發誓要繼續前進。十二天後的五月十六日，她登上了峰頂，成為史上第一位登頂的女性。這項成就史無前例，也開始改變世人看待女性登山者的眼光。
到了 1992 年，她成為第一位登上七大洲最高峰的女性。身為資深登山家，她也越來越擔心遊客在聖母峰上留下的垃圾。她重返大學，以這個問題撰寫論文，並花了多年時間努力保護她所熱愛的高山荒野。
她的故事凸顯了一個簡單的道理：峰頂是一步一步走上去的。在高山上晴朗的夜晚，星星看起來壯觀無比，幾乎近得伸手可及。然而，即使站在最高的山頂，天空依然高高在上。對每個朝著艱難目標努力的人來說，那幅景象傳達了一個訊息：每一座峰頂，也都是新的起點。攀登很辛苦，但永遠值得。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The history of climbing clubs in Japan
How companies decide which climbers to support
A woman who overcame many difficulties to reach the top of Everest and beyond
Why climbing Everest has become too dangerous
questions.explain: 文章敘述田部井淳子如何面對偏見、找不到贊助、遭遇雪崩，最後成為第一位登頂聖母峰的女性，並繼續完成七大洲最高峰與保護山林，故選 (C)。(A) 她創立登山社只是第二段的一部分。
questions.evidence: Her journey to the top of Mount Everest is a story of courage, patience, and a refusal to give up.

questions.stem: Why was it hard for the team to find a sponsor?
options: Many companies were wary of supporting women in a dangerous activity.
The team did not want any help from companies.
Tabei had never climbed a mountain before.
Everest was closed to foreign climbers at that time.
questions.explain: 第二段說許多公司對於支持女性從事如此危險的活動抱持戒心，所以很難找到贊助者，故選 (A)。(C) 與第二段她十歲就開始登山不符。
questions.evidence: many companies were wary of supporting women in such a dangerous activity

questions.stem: What does the author suggest in the last paragraph?
options: Climbers should only climb at night.
Reaching one goal can lead to new goals.
The stars are the main reason people climb mountains.
It is better to choose easy goals.
questions.explain: 最後一段說即使站在最高峰，天空依然高高在上，每一座峰頂也都是新的起點，暗示達成一個目標後還有新的目標，故選 (B)。(D) 與「攀登很辛苦，但永遠值得」的態度相反。
questions.evidence: every summit is also a new starting point

questions.stem: The word "torment" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 下文描述幾乎垂直的冰壁和雪崩，可知攀登過程極為痛苦，torment 指「折磨」，故選 (B)。(A)(D) 都與這些艱難的描述相反。
questions.evidence: The climb itself was a torment.

vocab.stem: To study in the United States, Amy had to apply for a student ______ first.
vocab.explain: 到美國留學必須先申請學生「簽證」，故選 visa。voucher（禮券；憑證）、verdict（判決）、vinegar（醋）都不能用來表示入境許可。

vocab.stem: Everyone laughed at the speaker's ______ remarks about her first day as a teacher.
vocab.explain: 大家聽了講者「機智風趣」的話都笑了，故選 witty。vertical（垂直的）、virtual（虛擬的）、wary（小心的）都無法讓人發笑，也不適合修飾 remarks。
